Step 3 — Needlet-domain architecture (localization retained, now survey- and likelihood-consistent)
3.1 Spin-1 needlet transform: transform the vector proper-motion field into spin-1 needlet coefficients β_{j,k} (band j, spatial index k). Use a specified needlet construction (e.g., compactly supported window b_j(ℓ) with overlap) and choose j-bands to emphasize low multipoles where the astrometric HD/TT signature is concentrated, while allowing localized downweighting of contaminated sky regions.
3.2 Data model in needlet space: write β = B d, where B is the linear needlet transform. Then
    Cov(β) = B C_tot B^T.
Exploit the structure C_tot = N0 + AΣ_aA^T + S_TT(θ) to compute matrix-vector products efficiently (diagonal + low-rank + structured signal).
3.3 No “full cross-source whitening” claim: implement inference using either (i) iterative solvers for C_tot^{-1}·v in needlet space or (ii) Woodbury identities for the low-rank nuisance term:
    (N0 + AΣ_aA^T)^{-1} = N0^{-1} − N0^{-1}A(Σ_a^{-1}+A^TN0^{-1}A)^{-1}A^TN0^{-1}.
This yields exact marginalization/weighting under the assumed generative model without needing unavailable Gaia pairwise covariances.

Step 4 — Exact likelihood and optimal detection statistic (addresses critique iv)
4.1 Gaussian log-likelihood: use
    ln L(θ_GW) = −1/2 [ d^T C_tot(θ_GW)^{-1} d + ln det C_tot(θ_GW) + n ln(2π) ].
Compute ln det via matrix determinant lemma for the nuisance low-rank part plus stochastic trace/log-det estimators if needed for the signal-dependent part.
4.2 Optimal quadratic estimator (optional implementation path): derive an optimal quadratic estimator for an amplitude parameter A_GW (or bandpowers) using
    \hat{A} ∝ d^T C^{-1} (∂C/∂A) C^{-1} d − Tr[C^{-1}(∂C/∂A)],
with Fisher normalization F = 1/2 Tr[C^{-1}(∂C/∂A)C^{-1}(∂C/∂A)]. This is the rigorous form corresponding to a properly normalized likelihood expansion.
4.3 Calibrated SNR and false-alarm: define SNR from either (i) likelihood ratio test statistic 2Δln L or (ii) \hat{A}/σ_A from Fisher theory, and calibrate its null distribution using end-to-end simulations that include the nuisance-mode prior and scanning-law templates.

Step 5 — Astrometric HD curve as a derived diagnostic, not the primary estimator (aligns with Asset 1)
5.1 From posterior/predicted C_ℓ^{EE/BB} to real-space correlation: compute the implied astrometric HD-like angular correlation function (proper-motion correlation vs separation) from the inferred TT signal model, including the survey window coupling. Use this as an interpretable diagnostic and cross-check against prior HD-curve approaches, but avoid using binned pair correlations as the primary likelihood object.
5.2 Systematics localization: exploit needlet localization to produce sky maps of residuals and jackknife stability metrics (drop-one-patch, rotate mask, scan-phase splits) to identify scan-synchronous contamination.

Step 6 — Astrophysical spectral model and identifiability (addresses critique v)
6.1 Baseline SGWB model: adopt Ω_GW(f) = Ω_BH(f; θ_BH) + η_NS Ω_NS(f; θ_NS, EOS), with η_NS ∈ [0,1] an explicit fractional amplitude parameter controlling the NS contribution.
6.2 EOS role re-scoped: EOS enters only through a constrained family of Ω_NS(f) shapes/amplitudes consistent with causality and maximum NS mass constraints. The primary deliverable is an upper limit or consistency bound on η_NS (or on an integrated NS contribution) rather than a claim of EOS measurement.
6.3 Fisher/identifiability study (mandatory): compute Fisher matrices (or simulation-based posteriors) for parameters {A_BH, α_BH, η_NS, …} under Gaia’s effective window W(f). Quantify degeneracies and demonstrate under what conditions (if any) Gaia can distinguish an NS-shaped component from an SMBHB-like power law. If identifiability is weak, freeze NS spectral shape and report only an upper limit on η_NS conditioned on EOS-feasible priors.

Step 7 — Validation program (explicitly tied to reviewer concerns)
7.1 End-to-end simulations with scanning-law systematics: generate synthetic catalogs with actual quasar sky positions, realistic per-source covariances, and injected nuisance modes A a drawn from Σ_a, plus optional additional scan-synchronous templates not included in A to test robustness.
7.2 SGWB injections: inject TT SGWB realizations consistent with the astrometric response, spanning amplitudes around current constraints (Asset 1) and spectral shapes motivated by PTA results (Asset 2) to test recovery and bias.
7.3 Transfer function and signal loss: measure the recovered amplitude vs injected amplitude to estimate the estimator transfer function under masking/mode coupling; require bias < predefined tolerance and quantify leakage into null combinations.
7.4 Benchmarking: compare against (i) quadrupolar VSH fits and (ii) pair-binned astrometric HD curves on identical simulations. Report SNR at fixed false-alarm, bias/variance on h_c and Ω_GW, and susceptibility to nuisance contamination.

Step 8 — Deliverables
8.1 A publicly documented pipeline implementing: (i) nuisance-mode construction A and Σ_a inference, (ii) TT forward covariance with window coupling, (iii) needlet-domain likelihood / quadratic estimator with Woodbury acceleration, (iv) simulation and calibration suite.
8.2 Science outputs: calibrated constraints on h_c(f_ref) and W(f)-weighted Ω_GW, plus derived astrometric HD-like correlation curves with uncertainty bands, and (if identifiable) a constrained bound on η_NS under EOS-feasible families.
Feasibility: 1) Consistency with actual Gaia products (addresses covariance realism): The revised approach no longer assumes unavailable catalog-level cross-source covariances. It uses only released per-source covariances (block-diagonal N0) plus an explicit low-rank generative model AΣ_aA^T for global/scan-synchronous correlations, which is exactly the regime where Gaia systematics are expected to dominate at low multipoles. Weighting/inversion is done via Woodbury identities and iterative linear algebra, making the method computationally feasible for ~10^6 sources.

2) Bias control vs ‘empirical N’ (addresses critique i–ii): By restricting correlated noise to a low-dimensional nuisance subspace with priors and by marginalizing analytically, we prevent an unconstrained empirical covariance from absorbing the SGWB signal. This is a standard, reviewer-aligned strategy: systematics are treated as parameterized modes rather than as free spatial covariance estimated from the same data.

3) TT treatment under masking and anisotropic noise (addresses critique iii): TT is enforced through a forward covariance model plus explicit window/mode-coupling, not by a hard map-level nulling. The estimator’s transfer function and leakage are measured in simulations and reported, ensuring that any signal attenuation from masking is quantified and corrected (or folded into uncertainties).

4) Statistical rigor and calibrated detection claims (addresses critique iv): The proposal now uses the exact Gaussian likelihood (including log-determinants) or a rigorously derived optimal quadratic estimator with Fisher normalization. Detection significance is calibrated against the null via end-to-end simulations containing the same nuisance priors and scan-law templates, enabling controlled false-alarm rates.

5) EOS claims made realistic (addresses critique v): Because Gaia’s response is effectively broadband and ultra-low-frequency with limited spectral resolution, the revised scope treats the neutron-star/EOS component primarily as a constrained sub-dominant contribution (η_NS) and provides an explicit identifiability/Fisher analysis. The deliverable becomes an EOS-consistent bound/consistency check rather than an over-strong claim of EOS inference unless the identifiability study demonstrates otherwise.

6) Strong continuity with prior art (Assets 1–2): The pipeline preserves the astrometric HD logic and connects directly to h_c and Ω_GW constraints (Asset 1), while adopting the PTA-style emphasis on properly normalized detection statistics, noise/systematics modeling, and SNR calibration (Asset 2).
final_critique: The methodological direction is strong and, in principle, aligned with how one should treat Gaia’s dominant low-ℓ systematics (explicit low-dimensional modes + analytic marginalization) while avoiding ad-hoc “empirical N” that can absorb SGWB correlations. However, several key elements remain under-specified at the level needed to justify the claimed optimality and bias control: (i) identifiability between TT signal covariance and the chosen nuisance subspace is asserted but not demonstrated—low-ℓ TT correlations can be partially degenerate with low-order VSH/scan templates, and the proposal lacks a concrete orthogonality/degeneracy metric and a mode-selection protocol tied to false-alarm control; (ii) the forward TT response is described at the level of pseudo-Cℓ coupling, but the actual catalog-level operator from a stochastic metric perturbation to mission-window-averaged proper motions (including time-domain response W(f), source sampling, and the E/B structure actually observable with Gaia) is not spelled out with enough mathematical specificity to assess correctness and implementability; (iii) the likelihood is labeled “exact Gaussian,” yet the computational plan for ln det and C^{-1} with ~10^6 sources is still aspirational—stochastic log-det plus signal-dependent terms can be the dominant numerical risk, and the proposal does not commit to a tractable approximation regime (e.g., bandpower parameterization, low-ℓ truncation, or explicitly low-rank signal model) with controlled error; (iv) the needlet layer adds complexity but the proposal does not prove it preserves optimality relative to a direct harmonic-space quadratic estimator given anisotropic noise and masking; without a clear argument, needlets risk becoming an aesthetic choice rather than a rigorously motivated compression. Overall, the proposal is logically coherent and well-motivated, but the strongest claims (higher calibrated SNR, less bias) require explicit, quantitative degeneracy analyses and a fully specified forward model and computational scaling plan.

original_chain: superheavy nuclides -> superheavy element -> nuclear decay -> nuclear astrophysics -> nuclear decay
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Superheavy nuclides (Z≥104) synthesized in a subset of neutron-star-merger ejecta produce a measurable, falsifiable distortion in late-time kilonova heating that arises from transport—not from the instantaneous-local-thermalization approximation—because spontaneous-fission fragments inject energy in a high-dE/dx, high-rigidity charged-particle channel whose deposition depth and time-delay depend differently on expansion, ionization state, and magnetic trapping than the beta/gamma channels that dominate actinide-only scenarios. The key claim is not that nuclear uncertainties are bypassed, but that (i) for any physically allowed superheavy source term consistent with broad priors on half-lives/branching and fission fragment spectra, the mapping from ‘injected decay power’ to ‘deposited heat’ is constrained by first-principles charged-particle slowing-down and pitch-angle scattering in expanding, partially ionized plasma, yielding a restricted family of deposition kernels; and (ii) this family produces a distinctive, testable pattern in multi-band light curves and nebular-phase spectra: a late-time color/bolometric evolution that requires simultaneously (a) enhanced charged-particle deposition relative to gamma deposition and (b) a temporally non-local heat release (delayed deposition tail) that cannot be matched, after marginalization, by actinide-only decay plus standard uncertainties (opacity evolution, gamma escape, ejecta stratification) or by smooth central-engine injection. We will demonstrate identifiability via Bayesian model comparison on synthetic and real datasets, explicitly propagating superheavy nuclear-input uncertainty through a kernel-operator formalism coupled to multi-D radiative transfer without double counting.
Plan: Step 1 — Ejecta ensemble (astrophysical state space, controlled):
1.1 Build a physically constrained ejecta ensemble using numerical-relativity-informed parameterizations: total dynamical+wind mass M_ej∈[10^-3,10^-1] M_sun, velocity field v(r,θ) with homologous expansion v∝r after t0≈10–100 s, and axisymmetric density ρ(r,θ,t)=ρ0(θ)(t/t0)^-3.
1.2 Enforce causality-respecting equations of state through priors on compactness and tidal deformability (consistent with GW170817-like constraints), but keep macroscopic ejecta parameters free in inference to avoid over-conditioning.
1.3 Generate thermodynamic trajectories (entropy s, electron fraction Ye, expansion timescale τ) using a low-dimensional surrogate that spans: (A) lanthanide-poor, (B) lanthanide-rich, and (C) low-entropy, very neutron-rich channels favorable to superheavy formation. Each trajectory set produces an abundance “source-term family” rather than a single yield.

Step 2 — Kernel formalism (operator definition + governing equations):
2.1 Define the decay injection field for channel c∈{α, β±e, γ, fission fragments}:
Q_c(x,t,E,Ω)=∑_i n_i(x,t) λ_i b_{i,c} S_{i,c}(E,Ω),
where n_i is number density of nuclide i, λ_i its decay constant, b_{i,c} branching ratio into channel c, and S_{i,c} the normalized emission spectrum.
2.2 Define the deposition operator K acting on Q to yield volumetric heat deposition:
\dot{q}_dep(x,t)=∑_c \int d^3x' \int dt' \int dE \int dΩ\; K_c(x,t; x',t',E,Ω)\, Q_c(x',t',E,Ω).
K_c is a Green’s-function kernel encoding transport, energy loss, and escape in an expanding medium.
2.3 Transport approximations by channel (chosen to be accurate at late times t≳0.5 d when non-locality matters):
• γ-rays: grey/energy-dependent Monte Carlo or deterministic ray tracing in homologous expansion with absorption+Compton effective opacity κ_γ(E) (including Klein–Nishina), yielding an escape probability P_esc,γ(t;E,θ). Deposit via Compton electrons locally where interactions occur.
• β-electrons/α: continuous slowing down with pitch-angle scattering; treat with a 1D-in-radius Fokker–Planck (or Monte Carlo) in momentum space including adiabatic losses in expansion.
• Fission fragments: treat as heavy ions with initial kinetic-energy distribution (two-hump TKE with prior), charge state Z_eff(v,ne,T), and stopping dominated by Coulomb collisions with free electrons + bound-electron corrections. Use a CSDA+straggling correction to compute stopping length ℓ_ff(E,t) in a plasma with evolving ionization.
2.4 Plasma state and ionization closure:
Compute electron density ne(x,t) from Saha or collisional-radiative steady-state using local temperature from radiative transfer iterations; where non-LTE is expected (nebular phase), adopt an ionization parameterization ne=χ_e ρ/(μ_e m_p) with χ_e(t,θ) inferred with priors informed by lanthanide recombination physics. Stopping powers use ne and Coulomb logarithm lnΛ(T,ne).
2.5 Magnetic-field trapping:
Include an effective pitch-angle scattering mean free path λ_mfp = η r_L, with r_L=p/(Z_eff e B). Parameterize comoving B(t)=B0 (t/t0)^-2 (flux freezing) with prior B0∈[10^3,10^6] G at t0=10 s (broad, covering weak to strong trapping). This modifies the charged-particle kernel by reducing radial streaming and increasing residence time; implement via diffusion coefficient D≈(1/3) v λ_mfp and solve a diffusion-loss equation in the comoving frame.
2.6 Numerical scheme and coupling without double counting:
Iterate radiative transfer and deposition in operator-splitting:
(a) Given T, ρ, composition → compute opacities and plasma ionization.
(b) Evaluate deposition kernel K_c and compute \dot{q}_dep(x,t).
(c) Feed \dot{q}_dep as the sole radioactive/decay heat source into multi-D radiative transfer (e.g., Monte Carlo packets or moment-based solver). Energy conservation enforced by tracking injected decay energy minus escaped energy (γ and, if allowed, charged-particle escape) equals integrated deposition + adiabatic losses; verify by global budget checks per timestep.

Step 3 — Superheavy nuclear-input uncertainty model (priors + propagation):
3.1 Abundance parameterization (explicitly not “bypassed”):
Represent superheavy contribution by a parametric mass fraction X_SH at reference time t_ref=7.5 h (motivated by Asset 2), with X_SH prior log-uniform over [10^-6, 3×10^-2]. Allow the rest of heavy species to follow an actinide-rich baseline abundance vector from a standard r-process network, but marginalize over actinide production via an “actinide boost” parameter A_act.
3.2 Decay-chain and fission priors:
For an effective superheavy ensemble, define hyperparameters:
• half-life scale τ_SH (log-uniform 10^3–10^7 s),
• spontaneous-fission branching b_sf (Beta prior favoring high b_sf but allowing low),
• mean total kinetic energy ⟨TKE⟩ (Normal prior 170±20 MeV),
• fragment charge/mass split parameter (symmetric vs asymmetric mixture weight),
• prompt γ fraction f_γ (uniform/weakly informative), and delayed β component amplitude.
These hyperparameters generate S_ff(E) and channel partitions feeding Q_c.
3.3 Fission recycling/yield degeneracy control:
Include a nuisance “recycling opacity/thermalization” parameter that captures secondary heating from fission daughters, but constrain it with nuclear-physics-informed bounds. This prevents falsely attributing generic extra heating to superheavy fragments.
3.4 Uncertainty propagation:
Draw joint samples of (X_SH, τ_SH, b_sf, ⟨TKE⟩, yield-shape params, B0, η, χ_e(t), ejecta structure) → compute K → generate light curves/spectra. Quantify which observables remain stable (low variance) across nuclear priors while differing between SH and actinide-only models.

Step 4 — Observables and identifiability (falsifiable tests):
4.1 Define the data vector:
• Multi-band photometry: L_b(t) in optical/NIR/MIR bands, with emphasis on t≳3–30 d where γ escape and charged-particle deposition diverge.
• Color evolution: e.g., (F200W–F444W) for JWST-like filters, plus optical–NIR colors where available.
• Bolometric reconstruction with uncertainty.
• If spectra exist: nebular-phase line blanketing/continuum slope constraints used as weak composition/temperature priors (not claiming unique line IDs for superheavies).
4.2 Synthetic-data retrieval experiment (mandatory):
Generate mock datasets from:
(A) actinide-only + standard thermalization,
(B) actinide-only + full transport kernel,
(C) superheavy+actinide with full kernel,
(D) actinide-only + alternative power source (magnetar-like smooth injection with L∝(1+t/t_sd)^-2) and dust/opacity evolution.
Adopt realistic cadence/SNR: nightly sampling days 0.5–10, then every 3–5 days to day 40; photometric precision 0.05–0.1 mag (ground+HST) and 0.02–0.05 mag (JWST).
4.3 Model comparison:
Use Bayesian evidence (nested sampling) to compute Bayes factors K=Z_SH/Z_noSH under full marginalization over ejecta parameters, opacity evolution (time-dependent lanthanide fraction proxy), γ opacity scaling, ionization, and magnetic trapping. Define detection criterion: ln K > 5 (strong evidence) and posterior mass on X_SH above a threshold.
4.4 Minimal detectable superheavy fraction:
From retrieval, report X_SH,min such that ≥90% of realizations achieve ln K>5 given the cadence/SNR above, as a function of (M_ej, v, κ(t), B0). This directly answers “minimum required mass fraction”.
4.5 Application to real events:
Validate on AT2017gfo and AT2023vfi/GRB230307A-like light curves (Asset 1 context): first show actinide-only models can fit early times; then test whether late-time data prefer transport-only corrections or require an SH component. Report posterior odds and whether X_SH is bounded or only upper-limited.

Step 5 — Robustness and degeneracy stress tests:
5.1 Opacity evolution: include κ(t,θ) parameterization tied to recombination and composition gradients; verify SH inference is not an artifact of κ(t) flexibility.
5.2 Freeze-out/non-LTE: include a nebular “inefficiency” parameter that reduces thermal coupling; test whether it mimics SH signatures.
5.3 Gamma escape: allow κ_γ scaling and non-grey effects; ensure SH preference is not simply reduced γ trapping.
5.4 Engine/dust: include alternative components (smooth central engine; dust extinction/emission) and compute Bayes factors with/without them.

Deliverables:
• A publicly documented kernel module implementing K_c with selectable MC/deterministic solvers and verified energy conservation.
• Posterior constraints (or upper limits) on X_SH and associated nuclear hyperparameters for benchmark kilonovae.
• A detectability map X_SH,min(M_ej,v,κ,B0,cadence/SNR) guiding future JWST/HST/ELT follow-up strategies.
Feasibility: 1) The proposal no longer claims to eliminate nuclear uncertainties; instead it separates (a) source-term uncertainty (yields, half-lives, branching, fragment spectra) from (b) transport physics that is comparatively well constrained. By casting deposition as an explicit operator K acting on an injection field Q, we can propagate nuclear priors transparently and identify which late-time observables are controlled mainly by transport (robust) versus by poorly known nuclear microphysics (non-robust).
2) The kernel is implementable with established methods: γ transport via standard Monte Carlo with effective interaction physics; charged-particle energy loss via CSDA/Fokker–Planck using stopping-power theory with explicit plasma/ionization inputs; magnetic trapping via a diffusion-loss formulation parameterized by B0 and η. These components are individually validated in adjacent contexts (cosmic-ray transport, SN γ deposition) and can be benchmarked against limiting analytic scalings (e.g., deposition fraction ∝ t^-2 for freely streaming γ in homologous expansion).
3) Identifiability is addressed head-on with falsifiable Bayesian model comparison under realistic degeneracies. The synthetic retrieval suite includes actinide-only transport, opacity evolution, γ escape, non-LTE inefficiencies, dust, and magnetar-like injection. The requirement is not a qualitative ‘mismatch’ but quantified evidence (Bayes factors) and a derived minimum detectable X_SH.
4) Empirical plausibility is anchored in the literature assets: (i) kilonovae with lanthanide-rich ejecta of order ~0.02 M_sun (Asset 1) provide the regime where late-time transport/escape effects are observable; (ii) nucleosynthesis studies indicate superheavy mass fractions can reach X_{Z≥104}~3×10^-2 at ~hours post-merger under favorable conditions (Asset 2), setting a physically motivated upper range for our priors; and (iii) reported late-time deviations from simple heating laws motivate testing transport-based deposition.
5) Even null results are publishable and decisive: if Bayes factors consistently disfavor SH contributions and yield only stringent upper limits on X_SH across events, this constrains r-process pathways and superheavy production in neutron-star mergers in a way that conventional instantaneous-thermalization light-curve fits cannot.
final_critique: This is an unusually sophisticated and technically mature proposal. Its strongest aspect is the clear separation between nuclear-input uncertainty and transport physics via an explicit Green’s-function kernel formalism, which directly targets a known weakness in kilonova modeling (the instantaneous-local-thermalization approximation). The transport treatments for gamma-rays, beta/alpha particles, and fission fragments are physically well motivated and internally consistent, and the inclusion of magnetic trapping and evolving ionization is appropriate for late-time ejecta. Logical flow from hypothesis to falsifiable observables is strong, and the identifiability strategy using Bayesian evidence and synthetic retrievals is exemplary. Minor weaknesses lie in the breadth of the parameter space (ejecta, plasma, nuclear hyperparameters, magnetic fields), which may dilute constraining power in practice, and in the reliance on simplified ionization closures (χ_e parameterization) that could partially reintroduce degeneracies the proposal aims to break. These are execution risks rather than conceptual flaws.

original_chain: globular cluster -> neutron star -> gravitational wave -> X-ray -> Doppler boosting
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Neutron-star binaries dynamically assembled and retained in globular clusters (GCs)—with enhanced retention supplied by low-kick accretion-induced collapse (AIC) progenitors—form a multi-messenger subpopulation whose early-time X-ray emission is frequently dominated by a mildly relativistic cocoon/wind component whose observed time–energy morphology is strongly modulated by special-relativistic Doppler boosting. The central claim is not that the neutron-star equation of state (EoS) deterministically fixes the outflow, but that the EoS induces *statistical* shifts in (i) the remnant fate (prompt collapse vs hypermassive vs supramassive NS), (ii) the disk/wind mass and velocity distribution, and (iii) the baryon-pollution/enthalpy budget that controls the attainable Lorentz-factor angular structure Γ(θ). These EoS-dependent shifts imprint a recognizable Doppler signature—joint spectral blue-shift and time compression (E→δE′, t→t′/δ) plus the beaming-induced hardness–intensity covariance—that is separable from intrinsic spectral evolution when modeled through instrument responses and absorption. We overcome the reviewers’ identifiability and overconfidence concerns by (a) replacing near-deterministic remnant→disk/B→Γ links with an uncertainty-marginalized, discrepancy-aware remnant/outflow emulator calibrated to NR/GRMHD simulation suites; (b) explicitly propagating emulator uncertainty and model discrepancy as hierarchical nuisance structure so EoS posteriors remain conservative under misspecification; (c) proving (via mutual information/Fisher and injection campaigns including upper limits) that Doppler-induced time–energy signatures remain identifiable against plausible alternatives (afterglow, fallback/accretion, magnetar nebula) across realistic observing conditions; and (d) aligning the amortized inference training distribution to the *observed* selection-biased distribution through a full yield forecast (LVK horizon × GC spatial distribution × follow-up completeness). This turns Doppler boosting from a nuisance into a partially identifiable latent variable that *probabilistically* couples to EoS through remnant/outflow statistics rather than through brittle deterministic prescriptions, enabling robust EoS constraints specifically for a GC-enhanced subpopulation.
Plan: Step 1 — GC-anchored population prior + yield forecast (selection-aware)
1.1 Build a GC catalog and spatial prior:
  - Construct a GC database for the Milky Way + nearby galaxies out to D_max=200 Mpc (not limited to ≤5 Mpc), including: sky position, distance, GC specific frequency S_N (host-dependent), GC system mass, and (where available) proxies for escape speed and central density.
  - For the Milky Way, ingest per-cluster escape velocities, core densities, metallicities, and pulsar/X-ray-binary inventories (Chandra/XMM), as in Asset 1, but use them to constrain hyperparameters rather than define hard event selection.

1.2 AIC-retention hypermodel (Asset 1 → NS retention prior):
  - Define hyperparameters Θ_AIC={f_AIC, σ_k,AIC, σ_k,CC, μ_NS,ret(M_gc), α_dyn} where σ_k,AIC is the natal-kick dispersion for AIC, σ_k,CC for core-collapse NSs, and μ_NS,ret is a retention scaling with GC potential depth.
  - Likelihood: use observed GC pulsar counts (and completeness-corrected millisecond pulsar and LMXB counts) with a hierarchical Poisson–lognormal model; map Θ_AIC to expected retained NS counts using an escape-speed-dependent retention integral over the kick distribution.
  - Output: a GC-conditioned prior on the number of retained NSs and a dynamical-assembly prior for BNS properties (mass ratio q, component masses, possible eccentricity at formation), with uncertainty.

1.3 Multi-messenger yield forecast (mandatory):
  - Define an *observed-event rate* for GC-origin BNS mergers:
    R_obs,GC = ∫ dV(z) [R_BNS(z) × π_GC(z|S_N) × p_det,GW(θ_GW) × p_follow,X(t_start, F_lim) × p_detect,X(model, θ_X)]
  - Implement p_det,GW using LVK detection efficiency surfaces (chirp mass–distance–inclination) from injection campaigns; implement p_follow,X via a cadence model (time-to-first-XRT/NICER pointing distribution, exposure distribution, sky-visibility constraints); implement p_detect,X by forward-folding model light curves through instrument response and absorption and applying detection thresholds.
  - Deliverables:
    (i) expected number of GC-origin events per LVK run (O4/O5) with credible intervals; 
    (ii) fraction of informative X-ray non-detections (upper limits) as a function of follow-up latency;
    (iii) sensitivity of EoS information gain to follow-up strategy (optimize cadence/exposure).
  - Crucially: use this forecast to define the *training distribution* for amortized inference (Step 4), ensuring it matches the expected observed distribution, not the astrophysical intrinsic one.

Step 2 — Data layers and GW handling (avoid lossy compression)
2.1 GW likelihood interface (mandatory rigor):
  - Primary path (preferred): ingest strain-level likelihoods through public LVK infrastructure where feasible (e.g., relative binning / reduced-order quadrature likelihood evaluations) to avoid summary-statistic loss, especially for (Λ1,Λ2)–inclination–distance correlations.
  - Secondary path (if strain-level access is infeasible for some events): use a validated *sufficient-statistic compression* via conditional density estimation:
    • Train a conditional normalizing flow q(θ_GW | d_strain) on LVK injection sets to emulate the full posterior over θ_GW={m1,m2,χ1,χ2,DL,ι,Λ1,Λ2}.
    • Validate by comparing Bayes factors and posterior moments against strain-level analyses for a held-out set.
  - Selection effects: incorporate p_det,GW(θ_GW) explicitly in the hierarchical likelihood and propagate its uncertainty.

2.2 X-ray dataset assembly (Assets 2–4 relevant):
  - Curate time-tagged event data (Swift/XRT, NICER, NuSTAR, Chandra) for confirmed counterparts and for targeted follow-ups yielding upper limits.
  - Standardize: absorption model N_H with host+MW components; consistent response matrices; background treatment; log-time binning with Poisson likelihood on counts (not fluxes).
  - Construct feature representation y_X that preserves time–energy morphology: binned count spectra over multiple epochs + hardness ratios + detection/upper-limit indicators.

Step 3 — Replace deterministic remnant/outflow mapping with a calibrated emulator + discrepancy
3.1 Remnant/outflow emulator (mandatory replacement of near-deterministic links):
  - Target outputs: latent physical quantities controlling early X-rays:
    ζ = {M_disk, M_wind(θ), v_wind(θ), Y_e(θ), baryon-loading proxy B(θ), Γ(θ) distribution parameters, engine lifetime τ_eng, radiative efficiency ε_X}
  - Inputs: θ_phys={EoS parameters, m1,m2, spins, mass ratio, remnant fate class, magnetic-field prior hyperparameters}.
  - Emulator type: multi-output heteroscedastic Bayesian neural network (BNN) or deep Gaussian process (DGP) with monotonic/positivity constraints where needed (e.g., M_disk≥0) and calibrated predictive uncertainties.
  - Training data: curated NR/GRMHD simulation suites spanning EoS variety and binary parameters; include multiple codes where possible to estimate code/systematic scatter.

3.2 Explicit model discrepancy layer:
  - Introduce δ_model as an additive/multiplicative stochastic process on emulator outputs, e.g. log M_disk = log M_disk,emu + δ_disk, with δ_disk ~ Normal(0, σ_disk^2) and σ_disk given a weakly informative hyperprior informed by inter-code scatter.
  - For Γ(θ): avoid deterministic B→Γ. Parameterize Γ(θ) with a flexible angular profile (e.g., core+sheath: Γ(θ)=1+(Γ_c−1)exp(−(θ/θ_c)^2) + (Γ_s−1)exp(−(θ/θ_s)^2)) and learn (Γ_c, θ_c, Γ_s, θ_s) from emulator outputs with uncertainty; allow δ_Γ to capture unresolved physics.
  - Propagate δ_model through the inference so EoS constraints broaden appropriately under outflow uncertainty.

Step 4 — Forward emission family: expressive, multi-model, selection-aligned
4.1 Competing early-time X-ray models (prevent misspecification → EoS bias):
  - Model A (cocoon/wind; Doppler-dominated): comoving spectral template (cutoff power law or synchrotron) with evolving normalization and cutoff; Doppler mapping analytic.
  - Model B (external-shock afterglow): standard synchrotron afterglow with energy E_k, circumburst density n, microphysics (ε_e, ε_B, p), structured jet parameters; includes off-axis geometry.
  - Model C (fallback/accretion X-rays; Asset 2): fallback rate ∝ t^{-5/3} with r-process heating modulation; luminosity capped near Eddington/super-Eddington with efficiency parameter; predicts plateau-to-decay behaviors.
  - Model D (magnetar spin-down nebula): spin period P0, B_dip, ejecta optical depth evolution controlling X-ray leakage; predicts delayed brightening in some regimes.
  - Implement as a mixture-of-models with per-event discrete label k and population mixing fractions allowed to depend on GC vs field channel.

4.2 Physics-embedded Doppler layer (retain, but now within mixture model):
  - For Model A, implement exact invertible SR transforms:
    E = δ E′, t = t′/δ, F_E(t)=δ^3 F′_{E′}(t′), δ=[Γ(1−β cosθ_local)]^{-1}.
  - Couple θ_local to viewing angle and outflow angular structure.
  - Forward-fold through instrument response and absorption to predicted counts.

Step 5 — Identifiability proof-of-principle (mandatory)
5.1 Mutual information / Fisher separability study:
  - Define parameter blocks: φ_Doppler={viewing angle ι, Γ-profile params}, φ_intrinsic={intrinsic spectral-evolution params, fallback/afterglow params}, and θ_EoS.
  - Compute (via simulation) the mutual information I(φ_Doppler; y_X | instrument, N_H) and the conditional MI I(φ_Doppler; y_X | φ_intrinsic) across instruments and realistic follow-up cadences.
  - Complement with Fisher-information calculations on simplified count models to show that the joint presence of (i) spectral shift and (ii) time dilation creates an identifiable direction in parameter space distinct from intrinsic cooling/fallback scalings.

5.2 Injection campaign with upper limits included:
  - Generate injections spanning: N_H distributions, response matrices, follow-up start times (0.1–10^5 s), exposures, distances.
  - Include scenarios where only upper limits exist in early epochs; quantify how upper limits constrain δ via exclusion of boosted high-flux solutions.
  - Metrics: posterior contraction on δ and Γ-params; bias on R_1.4 and Λ_1.4 under controlled misspecification; coverage tests stratified by model label k.

Step 6 — Inference architecture: CIMF upgraded with emulator/discrepancy and correct GW usage
6.1 Constrained Invertible Multi-messenger Flow (CIMF v2):
  - Latent variables z include: EoS c_s^2(ε) knot parameters; GW source parameters; remnant fate; emulator-driven outflow parameters ζ with discrepancy δ_model; X-ray model label k; GC-origin indicator g.
  - Structure: z → (emulator + discrepancy) → outflow parameters → (Doppler layer if k=A) → instrument-folded counts.
  - Training objective: amortized posterior p(z|d_GW, d_X) with explicit selection correction using the yield-forecasted observed distribution; include categorical k via Gumbel-softmax during training for differentiability.

6.2 EoS manifold with exact physical constraints (retain, but now uncertainty-aware):
  - Parameterize c_s^2(ε) with bounded transforms enforcing 0≤c_s^2≤c^2 and monotonic thermodynamic stability; impose maximum-mass constraint with a soft prior that reflects observational uncertainty.
  - Propagate EoS uncertainty through remnant thresholds used by the emulator; avoid hard remnant-class boundaries by using probabilistic remnant-fate outputs (e.g., P_prompt, P_HMNS, P_SMNS) inferred from emulator/NR fits.

6.3 Hierarchical population model linking GC channel and EM model mix:
  - π_GC depends on host GC specific frequency and Θ_AIC; allow GC channel to shift the prior on spins/eccentricities and on model label fractions P(k|g).
  - Joint likelihood includes GW detection selection and X-ray follow-up selection (cadence-dependent censoring).

Step 7 — Validation, robustness, and deliverables
7.1 Simulation-based calibration (SBC) for EoS and Doppler parameters under each emission model and under model mismatch; require near-uniform rank statistics.
7.2 Posterior predictive checks in time–energy space (counts domain) and cross-instrument consistency.
7.3 Sensitivity analysis: quantify EoS posterior widening when (i) discrepancy variances inflated, (ii) model mix broadened, (iii) GC-rate prior weakened.
7.4 Deliverables: public code for (a) yield forecast, (b) emulator interface with uncertainty, (c) CIMF v2 inference; release trained weights and documentation for correct selection handling.
Feasibility: Physics/astrophysics feasibility (addresses systematics): The revised design removes the proposal’s main over-identifiability risk by treating remnant→disk/wind→baryon-loading→Γ(θ) as an uncertainty-marginalized mapping calibrated to NR/GRMHD suites, with an explicit discrepancy layer capturing inter-code and unresolved-physics scatter. This ensures conservative EoS posteriors when the outflow physics is imperfectly known—directly addressing the dominant EM-side systematic identified by reviewers. The Doppler layer remains analytic and exact (SR), but Γ(θ) is no longer near-deterministic; it is inferred with calibrated uncertainty.

Model adequacy feasibility (addresses non-uniqueness of X-ray origin): Early-time X-rays in BNS mergers plausibly arise from multiple channels (cocoon/wind, afterglow, fallback/accretion, magnetar nebula). Instead of relying on a single comoving template plus a lightweight classifier, the proposal now uses an explicit mixture-of-models forward family with physically interpretable parameters and per-event model marginalization. This prevents structural misspecification from being absorbed into EoS parameters and allows conservative inference when the data do not discriminate.

Identifiability feasibility (addresses Doppler vs intrinsic evolution): The proposal now includes a mandatory, quantitative proof-of-principle: mutual-information/Fisher studies and large injection campaigns with realistic absorption, response folding, cadence, and upper limits. The separability claim is tested in the *counts domain* (not idealized flux space), ensuring it reflects actual instrument constraints. Upper limits are treated as informative censoring that can exclude strongly boosted solutions at early times.

Yield feasibility (addresses rate limitation): Rather than assuming a nearby (≤5 Mpc) GC-anchored sample, the plan provides a selection-aware yield forecast combining LVK sensitivity, GC spatial distribution (including host GC specific frequency), and realistic X-ray follow-up completeness. This forecast determines (i) whether the GC-origin subpopulation can be constrained in O4/O5 and (ii) the correct observed-distribution training set for amortized inference. The proposal also explicitly leverages non-detections and heterogeneous follow-up as constraining data, increasing effective sample size.

GW-feeds feasibility (addresses posterior recycling/summary loss): The proposal upgrades GW ingestion to either strain-level likelihood evaluation (preferred) or a validated conditional density-estimation surrogate trained and tested against strain-level analyses, explicitly preserving the tidal–inclination–distance degeneracy structure. Selection effects are incorporated in the hierarchical model rather than approximated by ad hoc efficiencies. This prevents the flow from learning artifacts due to lossy GW summaries.

Overall, the revised program remains ambitious but is now defensible: the EoS constraints arise from (a) rigorously preserved GW information, (b) Doppler-identifiable time–energy signatures tested under instrument realism, and (c) conservative marginalization over outflow-emulator uncertainty and emission-model ambiguity, with a selection-matched yield forecast ensuring the amortized training regime corresponds to what will actually be observed.
final_critique: Methodologically, the proposal is unusually well-engineered: it directly addresses prior identifiability and overconfidence failure modes through (a) a calibrated emulator with discrepancy, (b) mixture-model marginalization over competing X-ray mechanisms, (c) counts-domain response folding, and (d) explicit selection modeling for both GW detection and EM follow-up. However, two core scientific risks remain insufficiently resolved. First, the central separability claim—Doppler-induced joint blue-shift/time-compression producing a hardness–intensity covariance distinguishable from intrinsic evolution—may be substantially weakened by realistic spectral-shape flexibility, evolving absorption/partial covering, and cross-calibration systematics between XRT/NICER/NuSTAR; the plan mentions N_H handling but does not specify robustness tests against time-variable absorption or calibration drift, both of which can mimic hardness evolution. Second, the EoS leverage through early X-rays is still indirectly mediated (EoS → remnant fate/disk/wind statistics → Γ(θ) distribution → Doppler signature). Even with discrepancy terms, it is not demonstrated that the remaining conditional dependence of X-ray observables on EoS is strong enough to survive marginalization over (i) model label k, (ii) Γ(θ) flexibility, (iii) radiative efficiency ε_X, and (iv) ambient density/microphysics in afterglows. The mutual-information/Fisher and injection campaigns are the right remedy, but the proposal does not pre-commit to quantitative go/no-go thresholds (e.g., minimum expected information gain on Λ1.4 or R1.4 per event and required event counts under the yield forecast). Finally, the GC-enhanced subpopulation premise hinges on several uncertain steps (GC catalog completeness to 200 Mpc; host S_N inference; mapping pulsar/LMXB counts to retained NS numbers; translating retention to BNS merger yield). These are framed hierarchically, but the compound uncertainty may dilute the claimed “GC-specific” advantage unless the forecast shows a demonstrably higher informative-event fraction than the field channel under the same follow-up constraints.

original_chain: statistical component -> Kolmogorov turbulence -> geometric component -> Three-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence -> FRB 20201124A -> energy function -> frequency-magnitude relationship
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: FRB 20201124A’s (a) time-variable RM—including a periodic geometric component—and (b) apparent broken power-law burst-energy statistics can be jointly and *identifiably* explained by a single magneto-ionic environment if, and only if, we adopt a concrete forward model in which a 3D MHD turbulent screen simultaneously determines Faraday rotation *and* multipath propagation observables, while the intrinsic burst-energy distribution is governed by starquake-like statistics but is mapped to detected energies through a rigorously separated (nested) intrinsic–extrinsic selection operator.

Mechanistic core (what is new and why it fixes identifiability):
1) **Single-field forward model**: We posit a statistically homogeneous, anisotropic 3D magneto-ionic turbulence field with specified joint spectra of electron-density and magnetic-field fluctuations. From this *same field*, we derive both (i) RM(t) along the line-of-sight (LoS) and (ii) scattering/ depolarization metrics (τ_sc(ν), scintillation bandwidth, and bandwidth depolarization) via the *phase* and *Faraday-depth* structure functions. This directly answers the critique that RM is a LoS integral and cannot, without additional assumptions, predict transverse scattering: we make the assumptions explicit (cross-spectra, anisotropy, inner/outer scales), include additional propagation observables in the likelihood, and demonstrate via synthetic recovery when RM-only is insufficient.
2) **Nested E–RM operator with separable intrinsic vs screen effects**: We pre-register a minimal E–RM operator with two nested hypotheses: H0 (no intrinsic dependence of polarization coherence on energy; only screen-driven completeness) vs H1 (intrinsic energy modulates an internal depolarization parameter). We require multi-band held-out prediction to select H1. This prevents the operator from absorbing arbitrary selection effects and producing a spurious energy break.
3) **Formal identifiability and cadence aliasing study**: We explicitly test whether the proposed ‘cascade-consistency’ separation between geometry and turbulence is identifiable under the real cadence/gaps by simulation-based calibration (SBC), including adversarial cases where intermittent turbulence mimics quasi-periodicity.
4) **Demoted nuclear-physics claim**: We refrain from inferring EoS weights from radiated FRB energy. Instead, we produce conservative constraints on the *available elastic energy* (upper limits / consistency checks) under explicitly parameterized radiative efficiency and beaming priors; without independent anchors, we report posterior ranges conditional on those priors, not EoS model selection.

In this refined framework, the broken power law in observed burst energies is allowed to be partially intrinsic (starquake-like) but is *falsifiably* predicted to shift in apparent break scale with observing band/time-resolution if extrinsic turbulence-driven coherence loss dominates; the periodic RM component is predicted to be phase-coherent yet *non-cascade-consistent*, enabling separation from the intermittent turbulent component using diagnostics validated under realistic sampling.
Plan: A. Data construction (unchanged in spirit, tightened in specification)
A1. Unified burst-level catalog for FRB 20201124A across all available telescopes/bands:
- Inputs per burst: TOA, dynamic spectrum I(ν,t), Stokes Q/U/V(ν,t), fluence and S/N, time/frequency resolution, detection threshold model, calibration metadata.
- Include non-detections via survey sensitivity curves to avoid survivorship bias.
A2. RM remeasurement with a forward Q/U measurement model:
- Likelihood: (Q+iU)(ν) = (Q0+iU0) exp[2i(χ0 + RM·λ^2)] convolved with channel response; additive Gaussian noise per channel; allow for nπ ambiguity.
- Output: full posterior p(RM | data) + reliability score r_RM = 1 − P(multimodal or nπ ambiguous).
A3. Propagation observables per burst:
- Scattering: fit τ_sc(ν) from pulse broadening (where resolvable) using one-sided exponential tail or more general thin-screen kernel; otherwise upper limits.
- Scintillation: estimate Δν_d when spectral resolution permits.
- Depolarization metrics: (i) bandwidth depolarization across sub-bands, (ii) polarization angle coherence C_χ(Δν), (iii) frequency-dependent linear polarization fraction L/I(ν).

B. Mandatory Directive (1): Concrete joint forward model from a single 3D turbulence field
B1. Screen geometry and kinematics:
- Thin or thick screen parameterization with depth L and distance fraction s (source–screen–observer).
- Effective transverse velocity v_eff(t) = |(1−s) v_src(t) + s v_obs − v_scr| with priors: binary-orbital contribution for v_src(t) if geometry is present; bounded by plausible screen motions.
- Convert time lag Δt to transverse separation r = v_eff Δt.
B2. 3D anisotropic MHD turbulence specification (explicit spectral model):
- Fluctuations: δn_e(x), δB_∥(x), δB_⊥(x). Mean field B0 sets anisotropy axis.
- Power spectra (in 3D k-space):
  • P_ne(k_⊥,k_∥) = C_n^2 (k_⊥^2 + a^2 k_∥^2)^{−β/2} exp[−(k/k_i)^2] for k_o < k < ∞
  • P_B∥(k_⊥,k_∥) = C_B^2 (k_⊥^2 + a^2 k_∥^2)^{−β_B/2} exp[−(k/k_i)^2]
  • Cross-spectrum: P_{nB∥}(k) = ρ_{nB} [P_ne P_B∥]^{1/2}, with |ρ_{nB}|≤1.
- Parameters to infer (minimal set): (C_n^2, C_B^2, ρ_{nB}, β, a, l_o=2π/k_o, l_i=2π/k_i, L, s). Priors enforce physical ranges; β near 11/3 but not fixed.
B3. Derived observables from the same field (explicit links):
- RM along LoS: RM(t) = K ∫_0^L [n_0 + δn_e(x)] [B0,∥ + δB_∥(x)] dz + RM_geo(φ_orb(t))
  where K is the Faraday constant; RM_geo is the periodic geometric component (see Section C).
- Faraday-depth fluctuations and depolarization:
  • Faraday depth φ(θ) = K ∫ n_e B_∥ dz as a function of sky angle θ across the scattered image.
  • Bandwidth depolarization predicted from Var(φ) across the effective beam/image: p(λ) ≈ p0 exp[−2 λ^4 σ_φ^2] for external Faraday dispersion (Burn law), with σ_φ^2 derived from the φ structure function at the image scale.
- Scattering from electron-density fluctuations:
  • Phase structure function: D_ϕ(r;ν) = 8π^2 r_e^2 λ^2 ∫_0^L dz ∫ d^2q [1−cos(q·r)] P_ne(q, k_∥ integrated)
  • Define diffractive scale r_diff by D_ϕ(r_diff;ν)=1; then τ_sc(ν) ≈ (D_eff/c) (λ/2π r_diff)^2 with D_eff = s(1−s)D.
  • Predict Δν_d ≈ (2π τ_sc)^{-1}.
- RM time increments:
  • Use r = v_eff Δt to map temporal increments to transverse separations through the screen.
  • Predict RM structure function D_RM(r) from the spectra of n_e and B_∥ (including cross-term) under the same anisotropic power laws.
B4. Validation on synthetic turbulence cubes (required):
- Generate 3D random fields δn_e, δB with the above cross-spectra (FFT-based spectral synthesis), include anisotropy and inner/outer scales.
- Ray-trace or phase-screen propagate to produce synthetic I(ν,t), τ_sc(ν), and polarization with external Faraday rotation/dispersion.
- Sample synthetic data on the *actual* observing cadence/gaps and channelization.
- Demonstrate parameter recovery under three data regimes:
  (i) RM-only: quantify which parameters are non-identifiable (expected: C_n^2 and l_i poorly constrained).
  (ii) RM + τ_sc: show recovery of C_n^2 and β improves and enables τ_sc prediction.
  (iii) RM + τ_sc + depolarization: show recovery of ρ_{nB} and σ_φ improves.
- Pre-register success criteria: calibrated posteriors (SBC rank statistics near uniform), and out-of-sample predictive coverage for τ_sc and depolarization.

C. Mandatory Directive (3): Identifiability of geometric vs turbulence separation
C1. Geometric component model (explicit, low-dimensional):
- RM_geo(t)= Σ_{m=1}^{M} [A_m cos(mΩ t)+B_m sin(mΩ t)] with Ω=2π/P_orb; M≤3 unless data demand.
- Alternative: orbital-phase basis using known/fit P_orb with prior from Asset 1-like periodicity.
C2. Turbulence component model (increment hierarchy, now tied to forward spectra):
- Instead of an abstract multiplicative cascade alone, we use a hybrid:
  • Large-scale statistics constrained by the spectral forward model (Section B),
  • Intermittency captured via log-Poisson modulation of local RM increments: ΔRM(r) = ΔRM_Gauss(r) × exp(I_r), where I_r is a scale-dependent intermittent field with She–Leveque parameters (to be inferred) but constrained not to alter second-order scaling implied by β.
C3. Simulation-based calibration (SBC) for geometry–turbulence separability:
- Generate ensembles under: (i) pure turbulence, (ii) turbulence+geometry, (iii) turbulence with intermittent bursts that create pseudo-periodic runs, (iv) irregular cadence with seasonal gaps.
- For each ensemble, fit the full model and compute:
  • Geometry detection power: P(select geometry | geometry true)
  • False positive rate: P(select geometry | no geometry true)
  • Bias in inferred turbulence β, anisotropy a, and intermittency parameters.
- Pre-register acceptance thresholds (example): false-positive rate <5% at matched cadence; geometry amplitude recovered within 1σ for injected S/N≥X; and turbulence slope bias <0.1.

D. Mandatory Directive (2): Minimal, falsifiable E–RM operator with nested models
D1. Intrinsic energy model (starquake-like but not overinterpreted):
- True radiated energy distribution: p(E_rad) = broken power law with parameters (α1, α2, E_b), or tapered power law; fitted hierarchically with per-instrument completeness.
D2. Separation of intrinsic vs extrinsic polarization/RM measurability:
- Define a latent intrinsic polarization coherence parameter κ_int per burst.
- Nested models:
  • H0 (screen-only): κ_int independent of E_rad; p(κ_int) is stationary (or depends only on measured width/spectrum).
  • H1 (energy-coupled intrinsic): log κ_int = c0 + c1 log(E_rad/E0) with c1≠0.
- External screen predicts κ_ext(ν,t) from σ_φ and scattering predicted by Section B.
- RM measurability probability:
  P(RM reliable | burst) = sigmoid( a0 + a1 S/N + a2 κ_int + a3 κ_ext(ν,t) )
- Observed fluence/energy model includes detection threshold and scattering broadening loss.
D3. Falsification via multi-band break shift:
- If extrinsic coherence loss dominates the apparent break, then the inferred completeness turn-over energy E_turn(ν) must scale with ν according to the predicted τ_sc(ν) and depolarization scaling (approximately a power law tied to β and inner scale).
- Pre-register held-out tests: fit using one band, predict E_turn in another; compare H0 vs H1 by Bayes factors / predictive log-score.

E. Mandatory Directive (4): Nuclear-physics deliverable reframed
E1. Replace EoS-weight inference with elastic-energy consistency bounds:
- Model available elastic energy E_el ≤ (1/2) μ u_break^2 V_crust, with μ and V_crust ranges from representative EoS families but treated as broad priors.
- Introduce radiative efficiency and beaming: E_rad = η f_b E_el, with priors on η and f_b (log-uniform or literature-informed bounds).
- Output: posterior on η f_b required to reconcile observed E_rad distribution with plausible E_el; report whether extreme efficiencies are required (tension test), not EoS selection.

F. Inference engine and computation
F1. Joint likelihood includes: RM posteriors, τ_sc(ν) measurements/limits, depolarization metrics, and burst detection process.
F2. Sampling: SMC / particle MCMC with gradient-free kernels for non-Gaussian latent fields; use amortized surrogates (emulators) trained on synthetic forward-model grids for expensive phase-screen predictions, validated against direct simulations.
F3. Model comparison: (i) geometry only, (ii) turbulence only, (iii) turbulence+geometry, each crossed with H0/H1 E–RM operator; evaluate on held-out epochs/bands.

G. Deliverables and success metrics
- Demonstrated synthetic identifiability boundaries (where RM-only fails; where adding τ_sc/depol succeeds).
- Posterior predictive agreement for RM increment PDFs, τ_sc(ν), depolarization trends, and energy distribution across bands.
- Falsifiable conclusion on whether the observed energy break is intrinsically set (H1) or propagation/completeness-driven (H0) via multi-band predictive tests.
- Conservative elastic-energy/efficiency bounds rather than EoS weights.
Feasibility: 1) Addressing the RM→scattering underdetermination (reviewer point i): We do not claim RM uniquely determines scattering. We explicitly parameterize the joint spectra/cross-spectra of n_e and B (including anisotropy and inner/outer scales) and *include τ_sc(ν) and depolarization in the likelihood*. We then demonstrate with synthetic turbulence cubes that RM-only cannot recover key scattering parameters (expected), but RM+τ_sc(+depol) can—thereby converting an identifiability risk into a tested requirement on the dataset. This directly meets the mandate to “write down and validate a concrete forward model” and to show when RM-only sampling is insufficient.

2) Preventing the E–RM operator from absorbing selection effects (reviewer point ii): The nested H0/H1 operator makes intrinsic energy→polarization dependence optional and testable. By forcing model selection on held-out multi-band data—especially the predicted frequency dependence of the apparent completeness break—we prevent a flexible latent intrinsic term from mimicking propagation-induced breaks. This is a pre-registered falsification pathway, not a post-hoc explanation.

3) Geometry–turbulence separability under sparse cadence (reviewer point iii): We elevate ‘cascade-consistency’ from an intuition to a quantified identifiability statement using SBC under the real cadence/gaps and adversarial intermittent-turbulence scenarios. The outcome will explicitly state the parameter regimes (cadence, amplitude, intermittency strength) where geometry can/cannot be reliably detected, preventing overclaiming.

4) Nuclear-physics deliverable realism (reviewer point iv): We demote EoS inference to elastic-energy consistency bounds conditioned on explicit efficiency/beaming priors. This reframing ensures outputs are not prior-dominated EoS weights; instead, the proposal yields robust constraints of the form “required η f_b is within/outside plausible ranges,” which is scientifically valuable and defensible.

5) Alignment with Assets 1 and 2: Asset 1 motivates the presence of a periodic geometric RM component coexisting with stochastic turbulence; we preserve that concept but replace non-identifiable additive SF decomposition with a validated forward model plus SBC-tested separation. Asset 2 motivates a starquake-like broken power law in energies; we retain it while making the propagation-induced break hypothesis falsifiable via band-dependent predictions tied to the same turbulence field that explains RM, τ_sc, and depolarization.
final_critique: The proposal is technically ambitious and materially improved in identifiability discipline, but several key links remain under-specified or risk being non-identifiable in practice. (1) The ‘single 3D turbulence field’ is parameter-rich (C_n^2, C_B^2, ρ_{nB}, β, β_B, a, l_o, l_i, L, s, plus intermittency parameters and v_eff(t)), and the mapping from these to the joint set {RM(t), τ_sc(ν), Δν_d, depolarization} is not demonstrated to be uniquely constraining for FRB 20201124A-like datasets; in particular, L–C_n^2–l_o degeneracies in scattering, and n_e–B_∥ cross-term degeneracies in RM increments vs mean RM, are likely to survive even with τ_sc unless you impose informative priors or external constraints (e.g., screen distance, DM partition, independent velocity constraints). (2) The depolarization modeling mixes multiple mechanisms (external Faraday dispersion, bandwidth depolarization, scattering-induced PA decorrelation) but the proposal does not clearly separate what is predicted from φ(θ) statistics versus what is absorbed into κ_int/κ_ext; without a strict measurement model for PA coherence and L/I that accounts for intrinsic spectral/polarization variability, κ_int may remain a flexible absorber and weaken the H0/H1 falsification. (3) The geometric RM term is low-dimensional, but the ‘cascade-consistency’ separation hinges on correct turbulence scaling over the sampled time lags; real cadence gaps and limited dynamic range in Δt may make periodic vs intermittent discrimination fragile, and acceptance thresholds (e.g., bias <0.1 in β) are stated without tying them to required number of bursts, S/N distribution, or cadence window function. (4) The plan relies heavily on emulators for phase-screen predictions; however, emulator validity for tail statistics (intermittency, rare high-RM excursions, non-Gaussian depolarization) is not assured and could undermine SBC conclusions if the emulator smooths extremes. Overall, the mechanism is coherent, but the proposal still risks being underconstrained unless it commits to concrete external anchors and a tighter, testable measurement model for polarization/scattering observables beyond RM.

original_chain: binary neutron star -> spin -> remnant -> Virgo Collaboration -> neutron star
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Binary neutron star (BNS) inspiral data in the Virgo–LIGO network can yield *calibrated* (not prior-dominated) probabilities for post-merger remnant outcome—long-lived NS (hypermassive/supramassive) versus prompt collapse—when (i) spin-orbit and spin-induced quadrupole information is extracted with waveform models that explicitly include the relevant PN structure, and (ii) the mapping from inspiral parameters to remnant stability is implemented as a *probabilistic generative model* that marginalizes over EOS and over *model-error hyperparameters* (universal-relation scatter, NR-threshold-fit scatter, waveform systematics, and angular-momentum loss/redistribution uncertainty).

Mechanistic rationale addressing identifiability: while BNS aligned spins are typically small and degenerate with mass ratio and tides, enforcing EOS-consistent co-variation among {Λ(m), I(m), Q(m,χ)} does not act as a hard restriction but as a *correlated prior/likelihood augmentation* that reduces the effective dimension of the intrinsic-structure sector. This increases the mutual information between inspiral data and the remnant class by turning weak spin-induced quadrupole signatures (entering at higher PN order) into a *multi-parameter consistency test* against tides and masses. Crucially, the proposal does not assume the universal relations or NR threshold mass relations are exact; instead, it introduces explicit scatter parameters and checks posterior calibration (coverage) on NR injections across EOS and thermal prescriptions. The hypothesis is therefore: inspiral-only remnant classification becomes both informative and well-calibrated in a quantifiable SNR/parameter regime, because the pipeline (a) measures a constrained combination of spin–mass–tidal structure that is better determined than any single small effect, and (b) propagates all dominant modeling uncertainties so that P(prompt|data) changes only when demanded by the data (validated via prior-to-posterior information gain and coverage tests).
Plan: Step 0 — Define models, domains, and data products (pre-registered before analysis)
0.1 Events & injections: use public LIGO/Virgo BNS events (e.g., GW170817-class) plus a controlled injection grid spanning: chirp mass 1.0–1.4 M☉, mass ratio q∈[0.6,1], aligned spins χ1,χ2∈[−0.1,0.1] with additional stress-tests up to 0.2, and tidal deformabilities consistent with candidate EOSs. Include realistic PSDs across observing epochs; analyze both 2-detector and 3-detector configurations.
0.2 Waveform families (systematics control): analyze with at least two inspiral-capable models that include spin–spin and quadrupole-monopole (QM) effects: 
  • Primary: a PN/EOB inspiral model with explicit QM terms (e.g., an EOB family with tidal + spin-spin/QM support) using consistent PN order across comparisons.
  • Secondary (robustness): an alternative approximant with different resummation/implementation of tides/spin-spin (and, where feasible, an NR-hybrid injection truth model). 
Predefine the PN content to be included (spin-orbit up to the highest order available in the chosen model; spin-spin including QM; tidal up to NLO/NNLO as implemented).
0.3 Remnant labels for validation: for NR injections, define ground truth remnant class via simulation outcome (prompt collapse vs not), plus a standardized proxy for “long-lived” (e.g., survival beyond a threshold time) when available.

Step 1 — EOS ensemble and structure computation with explicit uncertainty
1.1 EOS bank: assemble hadronic + hybrid EOSs filtered by: Mmax≥2.0 M☉, thermodynamic stability, and causal sound speed c_s≤c (piecewise-polytrope or spectral parameterization). Maintain a *mixture prior* over EOSs (discrete bank weights or continuous hyperprior over spectral coefficients).
1.2 Precompute structure tables per EOS: TOV sequences giving R(m), Λ(m), I(m), and spin-induced quadrupole coefficient κ(m) (or equivalent parameterization used by the waveform). Provide interpolation with quantified numerical error.
1.3 Universal-relation model with hyperparameters: implement I–Love–Q / Love–Q relations as *probabilistic* constraints, not identities. Define hyperparameters σ_UR controlling relation scatter and possible bias terms b_UR (to absorb known approximation error at the relevant compactness/spin range). Calibrate (informative priors) using published residuals where applicable; allow posterior updating.

Step 2 — Likelihood acceleration with physics-coupled parameterization (relative binning + constrained transforms)
2.1 Relative binning backbone: implement relative binning for rapid likelihood evaluation seeded from matched-filter outputs (per Asset 1). Ensure it supports the chosen waveform families and the augmented parameter transform.
2.2 Parameterization: sample in (m1,m2,χ1,χ2, EOS or EOS-parameters, extrinsics). Deterministically map to (Λ1,Λ2,I1,I2,Q1,Q2) using EOS tables plus UR stochasticity: e.g., Q_i = Q_EOS(m_i,χ_i) × exp(δ_Qi), with δ_Qi ~ Normal(b_UR, σ_UR).
2.3 Replace hard “rejects” with soft generative factors:
  • Causality/Mmax: implement as prior support for EOS parameters/bank membership (hard only at EOS-parameter level), avoiding sharp boundaries in event-level intrinsic parameters.
  • Spin breakup: implement a smooth penalty/prior p(χ|m,EOS) that transitions near χ_K(m,EOS) with width w_K to avoid discontinuities.

Step 3 — Probabilistic remnant surrogate model (explicit definition + uncertainty propagation)
3.1 Remnant surrogate target: model the probability of prompt collapse given intrinsic parameters and EOS:
  p(prompt | M_tot, q, χ_eff, χ_a, EOS, θ_rem)
where θ_rem are surrogate hyperparameters.
3.2 Functional form: implement a calibrated probabilistic classifier tied to NR-inspired threshold mass structure:
  • Latent threshold: M_th = M_th,fit(q, χ_eff, EOS; a) + ε_th, with ε_th ~ Normal(0, σ_th).
  • Prompt indicator via smooth link: p(prompt)=sigmoid[(M_tot − M_th)/Δ], where Δ captures transition width due to thermal support, angular-momentum transport, and NR classification ambiguity.
3.3 Calibration/training data: train a and (σ_th,Δ) on an NR dataset spanning q, spin, and multiple EOS/thermal prescriptions (as in Asset 2’s logic, but extending to treat EOS/thermal differences as contributors to σ_th and potential EOS-dependent terms). Split into train/validation; report domain of validity explicitly (q range, χ range, mass range).
3.4 Angular-momentum/energy budget as a latent-variable model (no hard feasibility cut):
  • Introduce latent post-merger losses/redistribution parameters η = {f_J,GWpost, f_J,wind, f_J,mag} with priors from NR/EM-informed ranges.
  • Use inspiral-inferred J at merger proxy J_merg (computed from the inspiral model at a reference frequency/contact proxy) with an uncertainty term σ_J,model capturing waveform/systematic error.
  • Condition M_th (or Δ) on an effective support parameter depending on J_merg and η, but keep this as a probabilistic modulation, not a veto.
3.5 Output per event: posterior over remnant class with full marginalization:
  P(prompt|d)=∫ p(prompt|θ,EOS,θ_rem,η) p(θ,EOS,θ_rem,η|d) dθ dEOS dθ_rem dη.

Step 4 — Quantitative identifiability / information plan (mandatory)
4.1 Injection grid experiment: for each point in (SNR, q, χ_eff, EOS) grid, compute:
  • Prior-to-posterior KL divergence for χ_eff and for the remnant class probability (or the latent margin M_tot−M_th).
  • Mutual information I(data; remnant) estimated via Monte Carlo across the injection distribution.
  • Bayes factors comparing models with/without EOS–Q coupling (i.e., σ_UR→∞ as “decoupled” limit) to quantify when the data prefers the coupling.
4.2 Prior-dominance diagnostic: define a criterion such as |E[P(prompt|d)] − E[P(prompt)]| > k·SD[P(prompt)] with k preset, and require that this occurs alongside a minimum information gain threshold (e.g., KL(P||prior) exceeding a preset value). Report the SNR and parameter regimes where the criterion is met.
4.3 Sensitivity to spin magnitude: explicitly map performance as a function of injected χ_eff (including realistic small spins) to show whether gains persist at χ_eff~0.01–0.03 or only at higher spins.

Step 5 — Waveform-systematics control and robustness (mandatory)
5.1 Multi-approximant inference: run the full pipeline with at least two waveform families (Step 0.2). Treat waveform choice as a discrete nuisance parameter or perform model comparison; propagate differences into systematic uncertainty on P(prompt).
5.2 Synthetic waveform error model: introduce a hyperparameterized phase-error term δφ(f)=∑_k c_k (f/f0)^{α_k} in a controlled basis (small set of coefficients) with priors informed by known model discrepancies. Marginalize over c_k in a subset of analyses to bound bias in χ_eff and the remnant probability.
5.3 “Universal relation bias” stress test: repeat inference on injections where Q–Love relations are intentionally perturbed beyond nominal scatter (simulate EOS-dependent deviations) and verify calibration/coverage remains acceptable when σ_UR is allowed to expand.

Step 6 — Calibration and coverage validation (mandatory)
6.1 Posterior coverage: on NR(-hybrid) injections across EOS and thermal prescriptions, evaluate:
  • Coverage of credible intervals for χ_eff, q, Λ̃.
  • Reliability diagrams for P(prompt) and P(remnant=NS), plus Brier score and expected calibration error.
6.2 Compare against baselines:
  • Baseline A: standard relative binning with independent tidal/spin priors and no remnant coupling.
  • Baseline B: remnant map applied in post-processing with hard-threshold M_th (to demonstrate calibration failures from hard cuts).
Report whether the proposed probabilistic model improves calibration and/or sharpness without overconfidence.

Step 7 — Hierarchical population layer with uncertainty propagation
7.1 Joint model: infer event parameters plus hyperparameters for the spin distribution and EOS weights/parameters, *and* remnant-surrogate hyperparameters (σ_th,Δ,σ_UR) with informative priors from NR residuals.
7.2 Selection effects: incorporate Virgo–LIGO detection efficiency as a function of masses/spins/tides; propagate into hyperposteriors.
7.3 Output products: for each event and in low latency, deliver (i) EOS-constrained posteriors for masses/spins/tides, (ii) P(prompt) with credible intervals, (iii) calibration-aware “informativeness flag” indicating whether the remnant probability is data-driven (per Step 4.2).

Step 8 — Low-latency implementation deliverable
8.1 Compute budget: preserve the Asset-1-style rapidity by: precomputing EOS structure tables; using relative binning; limiting the dimensionality of waveform-error basis in low latency; and using dynamic nested sampling with pre-tuned settings. Target: O(10–30) minutes for an initial remnant-probability product; deeper systematic-marginalized products within hours.
8.2 Release: a reproducible pipeline (containerized), with pre-registered validation metrics and automated calibration reports.
Feasibility: Identifiability is explicitly addressed quantitatively: the proposal commits to an injection-grid + information-theory forecast (KL/mutual information) and Bayes-factor comparisons between coupled vs decoupled EOS–Q models, producing a phase diagram of when inspiral-only data can move P(prompt) beyond the prior. This directly answers the concern that small BNS spins and degeneracies could render outputs prior-dominated.

Systematic-error risk is controlled by design: (i) at least two waveform approximants are used, (ii) an explicit, low-dimensional phase-error marginalization bounds bias from waveform modeling uncertainty, and (iii) the EOS–Q “universal relation” is treated with hyperparameters for scatter/bias rather than enforced exactly—allowing the data (and injections) to expand σ_UR if the relation is not adequate.

The remnant mapping is not a qualitative rule but a probabilistic surrogate with defined inputs/outputs, trained on NR outcomes and equipped with calibrated uncertainty (σ_th, Δ) capturing EOS/thermal/transport variability. This avoids overconfident or discontinuous posteriors. The angular-momentum budget is incorporated via latent loss/redistribution parameters and uncertainty on J at merger inferred from inspiral, eliminating hard feasibility cuts and the associated calibration pathologies.

Finally, feasibility in low latency is retained: the computational core remains relative binning + dynamic nested sampling (Asset 1), while EOS structure and surrogates are precomputed. The NR-based threshold-mass logic (Asset 2) is retained but upgraded into a statistically consistent component with model-error propagation. The result is a coherent end-to-end inference pipeline whose remnant probabilities are validated by coverage and reliability on NR injections across EOS and thermal treatments, ensuring scientific interpretability for EM follow-up and EOS inference.
final_critique:
Methodologically, the proposal is unusually well-resolved: it pre-registers domains, uses multi-approximant inference, includes an explicit waveform-error marginalization, and defines calibration/coverage metrics for the remnant probability itself. The central identifiability claim—weak spin-induced quadrupole information becomes useful when tied into EOS-consistent multi-parameter structure (Λ–I–Q) rather than estimated in isolation—is logically plausible, and the commitment to Bayes-factor tests (coupled vs decoupled limit) plus information-gain diagnostics is a strong safeguard against prior-dominated outputs.

Main deductions come from two scientific-risk areas that are not fully pinned down. First, the practical measurability of QM/spin-spin contributions for realistic BNS spins (|χ| ~ 0.01–0.05) at GW170817-like SNR is likely extremely limited; even with correlated structure constraints, the data may not meaningfully update the relevant constrained combination unless the proposal specifies (and demonstrates via Fisher/IMRPhenom/EOB mismatch studies) the expected magnitude of the identifiable phase contribution relative to calibration/noise and tidal terms. Second, the remnant surrogate hinges on NR-derived threshold fits and an approximate mapping through J_merg and latent angular-momentum losses; without an explicit statement of NR dataset coverage (spin, q, thermal treatment, resolution systematics) and without a demonstrated invariance of the surrogate across waveform definitions of “merger/contact proxy,” the σ_th/Δ hyperparameters may simply absorb model inadequacy in a way that preserves calibration but yields low sharpness (i.e., probabilities remain near prior except at extremes). Overall, the proposal is scientifically coherent and careful about uncertainty, but it may overestimate where inspiral-only data can be genuinely informative for remnant fate in the small-spin regime.

original_chain: proper motion -> mass transfer -> magnetic field -> poloidal magnetic field -> quasi-equilibrium end-state -> growth-time -> kink instability -> poloidal magnetic field
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Intermittent Roche-lobe overflow in compact binaries can generate (or suppress, via burial) a time-dependent large-scale poloidal magnetic component on a neutron star by advecting magnetized plasma and driving reconnection at the magnetospheric interface; when the injected twist/current exceeds kink-stability thresholds in a *specified domain* (magnetospheric flux rope / jet-launching column rather than the deep interior), the ensuing non-axisymmetric reconfiguration produces anisotropic mass and Poynting-flux outflows that carry net linear momentum. We further hypothesize that the *integrated* recoil from repeated episodes over the system’s characteristic age can reach a detectable fraction of the present transverse velocity only in a constrained region of parameter space (high duty-cycle, sufficiently magnetized stream, and sustained anisotropy), and that this parameter space is falsifiable by a pre-specified momentum-and-timescale closure: (i) a maximum recoil velocity from anisotropic ejection and electromagnetic (Poynting) rocket terms that exceeds the post-correction proper-motion uncertainty of specific targets, and (ii) correlated secondary observables (spin-down torque changes and/or orbit-timing signatures consistent with episodic outflows). This refined mechanism overcomes the reviewers’ concerns by (a) separating internal field rearrangement (no net momentum) from external outflows (momentum-carrying), (b) fixing where the kink occurs and therefore which dynamical equations apply (resistive GRMHD + force-free exterior), (c) providing a flux budget and explicit null hypothesis (field burial/ohmic diffusion) that predicts no measurable recoil, and (d) tying detectability to quantified uncertainties after Shklovskii and Galactic-acceleration corrections rather than treating proper motion as a vague ‘prior’.
Plan: Step 0 — Momentum-and-timescale closure (mandatory pre-coding gate; produces a go/no-go region).
0.1 Select 2–3 concrete target systems with published timing + proper motion constraints (primary: PSR J2051−0827; secondary: a black-widow/redback with tight µ constraints). Compile: distance d (parallax or DM model with uncertainty), proper motion µ±σµ, orbital period Pb, observed Pdot_b and its uncertainty, eclipse properties (proxy for outflow), and characteristic age/spin-down parameters.
0.2 Correct the observed orbital period derivative for kinematic biases to isolate intrinsic terms: apply Shklovskii correction Pdot_shk ≈ (v_t^2/cd)P and Galactic acceleration correction along the line of sight. Propagate uncertainties to obtain a conservative residual Pdot_b,int±σ.
0.3 Define detectability threshold for recoil-driven proper-motion imprint:
- Convert proper-motion uncertainty into transverse-velocity uncertainty: σ(v_t)=4.74 d(kpc) σµ(mas/yr) km/s.
- Require predicted accumulated recoil Δv_rec to satisfy Δv_rec ≥ max[3σ(v_t), 0.1 v_t] (the latter prevents claiming significance when natal/systemic velocity dominates).
0.4 Explicit momentum budget (upper bounds and realistic bounds), distinguishing momentum carriers:
(A) Anisotropic mass ejection (wind/jet): for each episode i with ejected mass Δm_i and asymmetry factor η_m (0–1), momentum impulse Δp_m,i ≤ η_m Δm_i v_out. Adopt v_out ∈ [v_esc, 0.3c] depending on launch model (magneto-centrifugal vs relativistic pair wind).
(B) Electromagnetic rocket (anisotropic Poynting flux): Δp_EM,i = (η_EM E_EM,i)/c with η_EM parameterizing hemispheric anisotropy of Poynting flux (validated from simulation; conservative prior η_EM≤0.1). E_EM,i is integrated outgoing EM energy during the instability/outflow episode.
(C) Total recoil after N episodes over time T: Δv_rec = |Σ_i(Δp_m,i+Δp_EM,i)|/M_sys; include random-walk vs coherent-bias cases by bracketing: (i) coherent anisotropy (upper bound ∝N), (ii) stochastic sign flips (∝√N).
0.5 Duty-cycle and episode count constraints from binary evolution: tie N and Δm_i to mass-transfer rate Ṁ(t) and duty cycle f_d using Δm_i ≈ Ṁ Δt_on and N ≈ f_d T/Δt_on. Use plausible Ṁ from LMXB/black-widow ablation constraints and eclipse-derived column densities to set priors.
0.6 Flux budget & topology closure:
- Stream/companion flux available per episode: Φ_inj ≈ f_Φ B_comp A_stream, where B_comp is companion surface field (prior range 1–10^3 G for low-mass; up to 10^6–10^8 G for magnetic WD channel), A_stream is cross-section at L1/magnetopause, and f_Φ is the fraction of coherent net polarity that survives reconnection/turbulence.
- Compare Φ_inj to NS open flux Φ_NS ≈ π R_NS^2 B_p,NS and to flux needed to form a magnetospheric rope with twist > kink threshold.
- Null hypothesis (field burial): for high Ṁ and low f_Φ, accreted plasma advects/buries the pre-existing dipole; predict reduced external B_p and suppressed outflows/anisotropy ⇒ Δv_rec below detectability.
