  • Radiation-reaction consistency: verify that varying χrad at fixed σ and bg reproduces expected transitions from acceleration-limited to cooling-limited regimes.

SECTION 4 — Inference and identifiability-delimited deliverables
4.1 Bayesian inference with identifiability-aware parameterization:
  • Re-parameterize in terms of the combinations actually constrained by early data (from Section 0.4), e.g., A≡L0/Γ5 and B controlling Ecut(t), rather than naïvely sampling highly degenerate primitives.
  • Nested sampling for evidence among competing models.
4.2 Model comparison set:
  (A) POREC magnetosphere + pair-photosphere transparency sweep;
  (B) external-shock-only (as nuisance baseline);
  (C) jet prompt + external shock without magnetospheric precursor/opacity-regulated delay.
4.3 Parameter-recovery study (mandatory):
  • Create a synthetic-injection suite across plausible θ; recover posteriors with Swift-like cadence/latency; quantify which of {μ-effective, Edrv} are recoverable vs only their combination with Γ.
  • Report a “recoverability map” showing the region where magnetic moments/driver energy are identifiable; otherwise, explicitly downgrade deliverables to constraints on combinations (e.g., μ2 f(ι)/Z_eff).
4.4 EoS-linked driver attribution with non-uniqueness explicitly handled:
  • Treat driver energy as a mixture model: Eavailable = Ecrust (tidal shatter) + Eorb (unipolar-inductor Poynting extraction) + Epost (remnant winding/jet internal dissipation), with hyperparameters giving fractional contributions.
  • Use priors informed by compact-binary magnetospheric-flare efficiencies (Asset 2: ~20–40% conversion of crustal-shattering energy to flares) and by magnetospheric X-ray efficiency benchmarks in compact binaries (Asset 1).
  • Deliverable becomes: constraints on (Ecrust fraction) and consistency checks against Love-number-informed strain-energy budgets; only claim EoS discrimination if the posterior requires Ecrust exceeding allowed maxima across EoS families.

SECTION 5 — Validation, robustness, and falsification criteria
5.1 Energy and opacity closure tests: Ensure time-integrated outputs respect injected work and that predicted spectra do not violate τγγ constraints.
5.2 Falsifiable predictions (for GRB 050509b-class events / future short GRBs):
  • A transparency-sweep signature: evolving Ecut(t) and correlated hardness–intensity behavior within the first ~0.1 s.
  • Scaling: Δt ∝ L Γ−5 (to leading order in the analytic approximation), providing a population-level test when early X-ray onset times are available.
5.3 Connection to compact binaries: Compare inferred magnetospheric radiative efficiency (LX / Pcircuit) with double-pulsar-like efficiencies (Asset 1), and with flare conversion efficiencies in compact-binary magnetospheres (Asset 2), to check physical plausibility.

Milestones (sequence enforced):
M0 (Months 0–3): Complete Section 0 analytic scalings + synthetic identifiability study + gated go/no-go.
M1 (Months 3–6): Implement instrument-aware likelihood and minimal POREC without PIC (use bounded phenomenological closure) to test end-to-end inference.
M2 (Months 6–12): PIC similarity suite + closure tables with uncertainties.
M3 (Months 12–18): Full POREC+PIC inference on GRB 050509b; model comparison and deliverables.

Feasibility: 1) Quantitative closure on the 30 ms delay: The revised plan front-loads an analytic derivation of Rτ≈1(E) and Δtobs (including whether diffusion matters) and explicitly maps the (L, Γ, β, εpk) envelope that yields ~30 ms. This directly addresses the reviewer’s concern that the central timescale claim lacked a scaling argument.

2) Identifiability and degeneracy control: We add a mandatory parameter-recovery study with Swift-like cadence/latency and then re-parameterize inference in terms of the combinations actually constrained (e.g., those entering τγγ and Δt). We also introduce additional opacity-linked observables (Ecut evolution, hardness–intensity correlations) rather than relying on a single delay point. This converts the ‘identifiability advantage’ into a demonstrated, falsifiable statement with a recoverability map.

3) Kinetic anchoring and PIC portability: The proposal now specifies the dimensionless similarity parameters (σ, bg, χrad, ℓ, pair yield, curvature proxy) that define the transfer from PIC to global circuit closure, and it commits to an explicit interpolation domain with uncertainty propagation and withheld-parameter validation. This directly targets the scale-separation and realism critique.

4) EoS-linked driver non-uniqueness: Instead of assuming a unique crustal channel, we treat the driver energy as a mixture of crustal, orbital, and post-merger reservoirs and only claim EoS discrimination when the posterior necessitates crustal energies incompatible with Love-number-informed maxima. This prevents overclaiming and aligns the EoS deliverable with what the data can support.

5) Empirical grounding: Magnetospheric X-ray emission at measurable efficiencies in compact binaries (Asset 1) supports a viable magnetospheric radiative channel, while compact-binary magnetospheric flare simulations with high conversion efficiency (Asset 2) motivate the availability of a strong electromagnetic pulse near merger. The proposal’s core novelty is to connect these to GRB-like compactness conditions where γγ opacity and pair loading are unavoidable regulators, yielding a predictive delay and spectral-evolution signature rather than a tuned efficiency.
final_critique: This is an unusually sophisticated and internally self-aware proposal. Its strongest feature is the front-loaded analytic scaling and identifiability gate, which directly addresses the central timescale claim (~30 ms) and the degeneracy criticisms that typically undermine magnetospheric precursor models. The opacity-regulated delay mechanism is logically coherent and physically well-motivated, and the mapping from γγ opacity to observable spectral evolution is a genuine degeneracy breaker rather than a post hoc fit parameter. The main weaknesses are practical rather than conceptual: (i) GRB 050509b’s early-time XRT onset and spectral constraints are sparse and partially instrument-limited, which may cap the achievable identifiability even with the proposed Fisher/SBI gate; (ii) the full POREC+PIC machinery is complex enough that schedule and integration risk is nontrivial, despite the staged milestones; and (iii) the assumed isotropy and quasi-steady comoving photon field in the analytic scalings may break down for highly intermittent magnetospheric dissipation, potentially perturbing the clean Δt ∝ L Γ⁻⁵ scaling. These issues justify small score deductions but do not undermine the core scientific merit.

original_chain: characteristic strain -> Pulsar Timing Residual -> Pulsar Timing -> V_{\rm ISS} -> Pulsar Timing
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a PTA timing model in which chromatic propagation delays are generated by an explicitly parameterized, advected phase-screen (or small set of screens) whose transverse motion is hierarchically constrained by scintillation observables (t_d, Δν_d) will provably restrict the space of chromatic timing fluctuations in a way that standard Gaussian-process red-noise models do not, thereby reducing bias and variance in the recovered achromatic gravitational-wave characteristic strain h_c(f). The key mechanism is not the mere use of Hamiltonian language, but the kinematic identifiability imposed by advection: under a thin-screen (or two-screen) approximation at distance D_s, the allowed timing-delay subspace is generated by spatial gradients and curvatures of the screen phase φ(x⊥) transported as φ(x⊥ − ∫V_ISS(t)dt). This yields a chromatic delay process whose temporal power spectrum is analytically tied to the spatial turbulence spectrum (e.g., Kolmogorov P_φ(k) ∝ k^{-11/3}) and the measured transverse velocity. As a result, the induced timing delays occupy a restricted, velocity-controlled manifold with a calculable low-frequency cutoff and chromatic scaling (∝ν^{-2} for dispersive and ∝ν^{-4} for scattering-induced delays), which cannot emulate an arbitrary achromatic red spectrum with Hellings–Downs correlations. By contrast, flexible GP chromatic models admit long-timescale modes unconstrained by scintillation kinematics and therefore can leak power into the GW channel. Treating V_ISS(t) as a noisy latent—rather than fixed input—ensures robustness to scintillation-model uncertainty, while explicitly quantifying when mis-estimation of screen geometry would reintroduce bias. The approach directly implements the Pulsar Timing → V_ISS → characteristic strain → timing residual chain as a generative, physically restricted inference problem.
Plan: Step 1: Explicit propagation forward model (derivation + prototype).
1. Screen geometry: adopt a baseline single thin screen at distance D_s (fractional distance s = D_s/D_p), with optional extension to two screens if required by data. Allow anisotropy via an elliptical power spectrum with axial ratio A and orientation ψ. Assume frozen turbulence.
2. Phase statistics: represent the screen phase φ(x⊥) on a 2D transverse plane with power spectrum P_φ(k) = C_φ k^{-11/3} exp[-(k/k_out)^2], where k_out sets the outer scale. Choose a truncated Fourier basis with N_k modes up to k_max set by the requirement that induced TOA delays be accurate to <10 ns at observing frequencies (analytic bound provided).
3. Advection: evolve φ(x⊥,t) = φ(x⊥ − r(t)), with r(t) = ∫ V_eff(t) dt, where V_eff is the effective transverse velocity including Earth, pulsar orbital motion, and screen motion.
4. Mapping to observables:
   (a) Dynamic spectrum: scintillation timescale t_d and decorrelation bandwidth Δν_d are computed from the phase structure function D_φ(ρ) and Fresnel scale r_F = sqrt(λ D_s (1-s)/2π). Validate that the truncated basis reproduces observed t_d, Δν_d to within measurement errors.
   (b) Timing delays: dispersive delay Δt_DM(t,ν) = (λ^2/2πc) ∇_⊥^2 φ evaluated along the LOS; scattering delay Δt_sc(t,ν) = (D_s(1-s)/2c) |∇_⊥ φ|^2, yielding ν^{-2} and ν^{-4} scaling respectively. Provide analytic scaling showing how temporal PSD S_t(f) ∝ f^{-8/3} above a velocity-controlled turnover f_v ≈ V_eff/L_out.
5. Prototype: implement a minimal end-to-end simulator (single pulsar, wideband) demonstrating that N_k ~ 20–40 modes suffice to reproduce both dynamic-spectrum statistics and induced timing delays at PTA precision.

Step 2: Hierarchical treatment of V_ISS(t).
1. Latent velocity model: treat V_ISS(t) as a latent variable with likelihood from measured t_d(t,ν), Δν_d(t,ν), conditioned on D_s, A, ψ. Include Earth and binary velocities deterministically.
2. Multiple screens: include a discrete screen-index variable with Bayesian model selection between one- and two-screen hypotheses.
3. Bias quantification: analytically and numerically assess how mis-estimated D_s or anisotropy shifts power into low-frequency timing modes.

Step 3: Identifiability and regularization argument.
1. Reachable subspace: derive the covariance of Δt_prop induced by advected φ and show it is rank-limited by N_k and has a fixed chromatic/temporal PSD tied to V_eff.
2. Comparison to GP: compute the effective prior PSD of the propagation-induced process and contrast with a standard power-law chromatic GP, explicitly showing suppression of f→0 power and lack of achromatic components.
3. GW separation: demonstrate analytically that no linear combination of ν-dependent delays generated by the screen can reproduce Hellings–Downs spatial correlations.

Step 4: Spin-noise treatment (focused role).
1. Model intrinsic spin noise with a two-component crust/superfluid system, but restrict its use to bounding achromatic red noise at the single-pulsar level.
2. Use broad, pulsar-agnostic EoS-informed priors (e.g., I_total ranges from universal relations) to prevent unphysical long-timescale torque noise, without claiming precise M,R inference.

Step 5: Inference and computation.
1. State dimension: per pulsar ~2N_k (~40–80) for screen + ~4 for spin; per epoch cost O(N_k).
2. Algorithm: Rao–Blackwellized particle filter for nonlinear screen states with analytic marginalization of linear timing parameters; nested sampling or parallel-tempered MCMC for GW hyperparameters.
3. Scalability: pulsar-wise propagation states are conditionally independent given GW parameters—parallelize across pulsars; target O(10^4) CPU-hours for a 5–10 pulsar pilot.

Step 6: Validation benchmark.
1. Compare against standard wideband + chromatic GP pipelines on identical simulated datasets.
2. Metrics: bias and coverage of recovered h_c(f), Bayes factors, and residual variance decomposition.

Feasibility: This revision directly addresses reviewer concerns by replacing qualitative claims with explicit derivations and constraints. The propagation forward model is grounded in standard thin-screen scintillation theory and wave propagation, with analytic scaling that ties timing-delay power spectra to measurable scintillation parameters and V_ISS. The low-dimensional basis is justified by outer-scale and precision requirements and is validated via a prototype simulator. Identifiability is formalized by characterizing the reachable delay subspace under advection, demonstrating mathematically why long-timescale achromatic absorption is suppressed relative to GP models. Treating V_ISS(t) hierarchically acknowledges its model dependence and allows direct quantification of bias from mis-specification. Computational feasibility is ensured through rank-limited state spaces, conditional independence across pulsars, and staged deployment beginning with a small pilot PTA subset. Overall, the proposal advances PTA analysis by converting scintillation from a nuisance into a physically constraining driver that sharpens inference on the stochastic gravitational-wave background.
final_critique: The core idea—using advection + scintillation-derived kinematics to restrict the chromatic timing-delay subspace—is scientifically well-motivated and plausibly addresses known GP leakage/overfitting pathologies. The engineering plan is comparatively detailed (state dimension, basis truncation, prototype, and inference machinery), but several physics-to-data mappings are oversimplified or risk internal inconsistency at PTA precision. In particular: (i) the stated timing-delay functionals (∇⊥²φ for DM and |∇⊥φ|² for scattering delay) conflate plasma dispersion (column density integral) with geometric/diffractive delays from phase curvature; you need a rigorous derivation showing which terms survive under the thin-screen approximation and which are already absorbed by standard wideband DM estimation. (ii) The claimed PSD scaling and low-frequency turnover (S_t ∝ f^{-8/3} with cutoff ~V_eff/L_out) depends sensitively on outer-scale, anisotropy, and whether the observable is linear (phase/DM) or quadratic (scattering), and on intermittency; as written it reads more like a heuristic than a provable restriction. (iii) The identifiability claim that the chromatic screen process “cannot emulate” achromatic Hellings–Downs-correlated residuals is directionally right, but not demonstrated at the level needed for a board: frequency-dependent systematics can still bias GW inference through imperfect chromatic separation, finite-band coupling, profile evolution, and mis-modeled dispersion/scattering degeneracies—especially when V_ISS(t), D_s, and anisotropy are uncertain. (iv) The proposal under-specifies the likelihood connecting dynamic-spectrum measurements (t_d, Δν_d) to the latent screen parameters/velocities, including treatment of measurement covariances, refractive modulations, and non-stationarity; without this, the hierarchical constraint may be too weak to meaningfully restrict low-frequency chromatic modes. Overall, the methodological direction is strong, but the proposal needs tighter derivations and a more explicit multi-pulsar end-to-end identifiability/bias analysis to justify the “provably restricts” language.

original_chain: compressive wave -> hot outflow -> compressive wave -> inclined magnetosphere -> Alfvenic turbulence
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in neutron-star systems with an inclined magnetosphere, Alfvenic turbulence generated at shear interfaces nonlinearly converts into large-amplitude compressive waves that seed a hot, magnetized outflow, with the efficiency of this conversion governed by relativistic mode-coupling constrained by the neutron-star equation of state (EoS). To test this, we propose a methodological adaptation that embeds a mode-resolved, energy-conserving turbulence closure into fully relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations, explicitly enforcing Alfven–fast magnetosonic coupling under causality and EoS constraints. This adaptation overcomes the limitation of existing force-free or ideal GRMHD approaches, which either neglect plasma inertia or under-resolve turbulent energy transfer into compressive modes.
Plan: Step 1: System setup and physical initialization.
- Construct 3D GRMHD simulations of a rotating neutron star with a tilted magnetic dipole (inclination angles 0–60 degrees), using multiple realistic nuclear EoS (soft to stiff) to span allowed mass–radius relations.
- Initialize a stratified magnetosphere with a low but finite plasma beta to allow both Alfvenic and compressive dynamics, and impose differential rotation or binary-induced shear to trigger turbulence.

Step 2: Methodological adaptation – mode-resolved turbulent closure.
- Augment the GRMHD equations with a scale-dependent turbulence closure that decomposes fluctuations into Alfvenic and compressive (fast magnetosonic) components using local relativistic Elsässer variables.
- Introduce an explicit nonlinear coupling term that transfers energy from Alfvenic turbulence to compressive waves when critical balance and resonance conditions are satisfied, while enforcing local conservation of energy–momentum and subluminal wave speeds.
- Calibrate the coupling coefficients using high-resolution local box simulations and analytically constrained by relativistic MHD wave dispersion relations.

Step 3: Validation and analysis.
- Quantify the radial energy flux partition (Poynting vs thermal vs kinetic) and identify the emergence of compressive waves and shocks.
- Correlate compressive-wave amplitude and hot outflow entropy with magnetospheric inclination and EoS stiffness.
- Compare synthetic observables (gamma-ray precursor energetics, fast radio burst-like timescales) against existing simulations lacking the adapted closure to demonstrate improvement.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Prior FFE and MHD studies demonstrate the presence of Alfvenic turbulence and outgoing compressive waves in inclined magnetospheres, but lack a controlled mechanism for their coupling. Relativistic MHD theory provides well-defined mode structures and conservation laws that anchor the proposed closure.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): By embedding mode coupling directly into GRMHD, the method respects causality, symmetry, and EoS-dependent inertia—critical for high-energy astrophysics and nuclear physics applications involving neutron stars.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike force-free or purely ideal GRMHD simulations, this adapted approach captures the mechanistic pathway from Alfvenic turbulence to compressive waves and hot outflows, enabling quantitative predictions of multi-messenger signals and their dependence on nuclear microphysics.
final_critique: The proposal targets a real bottleneck—ideal GRMHD/FFE typically do not provide controlled, mode-resolved turbulent energy transfer into compressive modes—and the idea of enforcing Alfvén–fast coupling with conservation/causality constraints is scientifically motivated. However, the engineering plan is underspecified at the level required for a turbulence-closure insertion into conservative GRMHD: it does not define the closure’s mathematical form, how fluctuations are separated from mean fields in curved spacetime (filtering/LES operator, gauge/coordinate dependence), how the added coupling term preserves hyperbolicity and the scheme’s conservative update, or how positivity (ρ, p) and divergence constraints (∇·B=0) are maintained when injecting compressive energy. The logic linking EoS stiffness to mode-coupling efficiency is plausible via inertia/enthalpy and wave speeds, but it is currently asserted rather than derived: in relativistic MHD the mode structure depends on magnetization and enthalpy, yet the closure triggers (critical balance/resonance) need explicit relativistic criteria and a demonstration that they operate in strongly stratified, magnetically dominated magnetospheres where the Alfvén speed is near-c. The calibration strategy (local box + dispersion relations) is reasonable, but the mapping from local homogeneous boxes to global, inhomogeneous, rotating, GR backgrounds is nontrivial and not addressed (e.g., how coefficients vary with magnetization σ, plasma-β, curvature, and frame-dragging). Finally, the synthetic-observable component (gamma-ray precursors/FRB-like timescales) is too loosely connected to the simulated quantities (no radiative transfer/emission prescription, no explicit linkage between compressive/shock statistics and observable signatures), risking overclaiming improvement.

original_chain: gravitational wave energy density -> characteristic strain -> signal-to-noise ratio statistic -> Supermassive Black Hole Binary -> Inter-Pulsar Spatial Correlations
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: If the nanohertz stochastic gravitational-wave background contains a GR tensor-mode component sourced predominantly by an astrophysical SMBHB population, then a detection statistic that (a) operates in the timing-model–marginalized, noise-whitened residual space, (b) explicitly projects cross-covariances onto an orthogonalized set of *effective* spatial kernels (HD quadrupole, monopole clock, dipole ephemeris, and optional beyond-GR/anisotropy bases), and (c) uses a robustness-first spectral treatment (paired constrained SMBHB-informed model and a semi-parametric alternative with weak regularization) will increase *true* detection probability at a fixed false-alarm rate while preventing biased significance under spectral mismatch. Mechanistically, the approach overcomes the key PTA bottleneck—leakage between common red processes and quadrupolar correlations—by enforcing separation where it matters statistically: after design-matrix projection and whitening under per-pulsar noise. In this projected space, the GLRT decomposes the cross-power into orthogonal kernel subspaces, concentrating evidence for HD correlations only in the component that survives both (i) timing-model marginalization and (ii) null-calibrated whitening, while simultaneously quantifying identifiability limits in mapping band-limited hc(f) to ΩGW(f) when SMBHB environmental coupling/eccentricity and population uncertainties induce degeneracies. The proposal therefore replaces claims of unique ΩGW inference with a falsifiable identifiability analysis and includes a guardrail against model-mismatch loss by running constrained and semi-parametric spectra in parallel and comparing their calibrated detection performance and coverage.
Plan: Step 0 — Data products and notation (pre-registered):
0.1 Use a PTA dataset with TOAs, timing models, and standard noise components (e.g., NANOGrav-like). For pulsar a, define post-fit residuals r_a and timing-model design matrix M_a.
0.2 Pre-register: (i) kernel set, (ii) spectral families, (iii) prior families and widths, (iv) null-calibration protocol, (v) diagnostics and stopping rules.

Step 1 — Timing-model marginalization and whitening (the space where kernels must be orthogonalized):
1.1 For each pulsar a, construct the projection matrix that marginalizes timing-model parameters:
  G_a = I - M_a (M_a^T N_a^{-1} M_a)^{-1} M_a^T N_a^{-1}
where N_a is the white-noise TOA covariance (EFAC/EQUAD/ECORR as applicable). Work with projected residuals: r̃_a = G_a r_a.
1.2 Build a scalable Gaussian-process likelihood in a low-rank Fourier basis for red processes. For each pulsar a, represent intrinsic red noise via Fourier design F_a with n_f frequencies; the red-noise covariance is F_a Φ_a F_a^T (Φ_a diagonal in Fourier coefficients).
1.3 Define the full projected covariance across all pulsars in block form:
  C = G (N + F Φ F^T + S(θ, spectral)) G^T
where S encodes spatially correlated processes (HD/monopole/dipole/optional). Implement whitening via Cholesky or iterative solves: define W such that W^T C0 W = I under the null model C0 (no HD term, but including fitted per-pulsar noise and monopole/dipole if desired). Use W to map data to whitened projected residuals y = W^T r̃.

Step 2 — Define *effective* spatial kernels and orthogonalize them in the whitened, projected space:
2.1 Start from theoretical sky kernels K_k(θ_ab):
  k ∈ {HD tensor, monopole(clock), dipole(ephemeris), alt-pol templates, anisotropy basis (optional)}.
2.2 Convert sky kernels into operators on the whitened data. In Fourier-bin i, the correlated cross-covariance contribution has the form:
  S_i = Σ_k A_{k,i}  (B_{k,i})
where B_{k,i} is the block matrix with (a,b) block proportional to K_k(θ_ab) times the Fourier-basis mapping for that bin.
2.3 Compute the kernel inner product in the *actual* experiment:
  ⟨B_k, B_l⟩ = tr( B_k^T  P  B_l  P )
where P is the operator induced by (i) design-matrix projection G and (ii) whitening W (equivalently work directly with whitened-projected operators: B̂_k = W^T G^T B_k G W).
2.4 Orthogonalize kernels using Gram–Schmidt (or SVD) under ⟨·,·⟩ to obtain an orthonormal basis {Ũ_m}. This ensures that “orthogonality” accounts for cadence heterogeneity, timing-model fits, and noise weighting—not just sky geometry.

Step 3 — Constrained GLRT derived in the projected/whitened basis (and its semi-parametric guardrail):
3.1 Parameterize the correlated signal in Fourier space. For each frequency bin i, model coefficients β_{m,i} multiplying orthonormal kernels Ũ_m.
3.2 Define two spectral families for the HD component (m = HD):
  (A) Constrained SMBHB-informed family: hc(f) = A (f/f_yr)^α × C_env(f; κ_env) × C_ecc(f; κ_ecc), where α≈−2/3 but allowed to vary in a bounded range; C_env and C_ecc are low-dimensional curvature modifiers (e.g., broken power-law turnover frequency f_b and smoothness η).
  (B) Semi-parametric family: free-spectrum with weak smoothness hyperprior (e.g., log hc,i with Gaussian random-walk prior or cubic spline with penalty λ). This is the mismatch guardrail.
3.3 Monopole/dipole/common processes: include monopole and dipole spectra in parallel as either (i) independent free-spectra with weak priors, or (ii) shared low-dimensional spectra, and quantify posterior covariance with HD.
3.4 GLRT derivation: in the whitened-projected domain, define the log-likelihood ratio between H1 (includes HD term) and H0 (no HD term) while always including timing-model marginalization and per-pulsar noise:
  Λ = 2[ max_{θ_noise, θ_corr∈H1} log p(y | θ_noise, θ_corr) − max_{θ_noise, θ_corr∈H0} log p(y | θ_noise, θ_corr) ].
Compute Λ for both spectral families: Λ_constrained and Λ_semiparam.
3.5 Decision rule (robustness-first): declare “HD-correlated detection” only if
  (i) Λ_semiparam exceeds a pre-registered null threshold (controls false alarm without relying on strong spectral assumptions), and
  (ii) Λ_constrained is not in significant tension with Λ_semiparam under posterior predictive checks (guards against prior-driven inflation), and
  (iii) recovered spatial structure places dominant power in the HD orthonormal component rather than monopole/dipole.

Step 4 — Identifiability analysis for ΩGW inference (replace “unique mapping” with quantification):
4.1 Always use the kinematic relation ΩGW(f) = (2π^2/3H0^2) f^2 hc(f)^2 for conversion, but explicitly report that PTAs infer ΩGW only over their sensitive band.
4.2 Quantify degeneracies by Fisher/likelihood geometry and injection-recovery:
  • Vary SMBHB hyperparameters (A, α, f_b, η, eccentricity proxy) and show posterior correlations and profile likelihoods.
  • Report which combinations are identifiable (e.g., band-averaged ΩGW, effective slope in-band) versus non-identifiable.
4.3 Cross-check with independent astrometric constraints by translating posterior hc(f_yr) to ΩGW(f_yr) and comparing to Gaia-like astrometric HD upper limits (as an external consistency diagnostic, not as a prior unless explicitly justified).

Step 5 — Neutron-star EoS / moment-of-inertia linkage (demoted to sensitivity study unless made predictive):
5.1 Primary analysis: per-pulsar intrinsic red noise remains empirical (amplitude + spectral index or free-spectrum), with hierarchical sharing across pulsars if supported by data.
5.2 Optional sensitivity module (non-decision-critical): implement a torque-noise-inspired prior family and test informativeness:
  • Define a mapping from torque fluctuations to spin-noise PSD with amplitude parameter A_torque and slope γ.
  • Use EoS-derived I bounds only to set extremely weak, order-of-magnitude constraints on A_torque (demonstrate via prior-to-posterior KL divergence that it is either informative or effectively ignorable).
5.3 Pre-registered criterion: if EoS-based priors shift the HD amplitude posterior or Bayes factors beyond a small tolerance without improving predictive fit, the EoS prior is excluded from the final detection claim and reported only as a systematic sensitivity result.

Step 6 — Scalable computation and complexity:
6.1 Use Fourier-sum GP methods (low-rank) so that per-pulsar red-noise covariance is handled via Woodbury identities:
  (N + F Φ F^T)^{-1} = N^{-1} − N^{-1} F (Φ^{-1} + F^T N^{-1} F)^{-1} F^T N^{-1}.
6.2 Exploit block structure across pulsars; avoid forming full dense cross-covariances in the time domain. Work primarily in Fourier coefficient space where correlated processes factor by frequency bin.
6.3 Complexity targets: with P pulsars, typical n_TOA per pulsar, and n_f Fourier modes, aim for O(P n_TOA n_f^2 + P n_f^3) per likelihood evaluation (dominated by small-matrix inversions per pulsar and per frequency bin) rather than O((Σ n_TOA)^3).
6.4 Sampling/inference:
  • Use HMC/NUTS for continuous parameters in the constrained and semi-parametric models separately (no reversible-jump in the primary claim).
  • Optional kernels (alt polarizations/anisotropy) handled via model comparison across a small pre-defined set, not RJMCMC.
  • Convergence diagnostics: split-Rhat, ESS thresholds, energy/BFMI; posterior predictive residual checks in whitened space.

Step 7 — Null calibration, robustness, and coverage (to prevent inflated significance):
7.1 Calibrate false-alarm using null simulations generated from posterior predictive draws under H0 that preserve cadence, heteroscedasticity, and timing-model projection.
7.2 Prior sensitivity: repeat calibrations under widened/narrowed priors for spectral smoothness and SMBHB curvature; report impact on Λ thresholds and Bayes factors.
7.3 Mismatch injections: inject (i) pure SMBHB HD, (ii) HD with environmental turnover, (iii) anisotropic backgrounds, (iv) nonstationary common red processes, (v) monopole/dipole contaminants, and mixtures. Compare detection power/false-alarm for Λ_constrained vs Λ_semiparam.
7.4 Coverage tests: for injected amplitudes, verify credible-interval coverage for hc(f_yr) and band-averaged ΩGW; flag any systematic under-coverage as evidence of over-constraining priors.

Deliverables:
D1. A derived, timing-marginalized, whitened-space kernel-orthogonalization procedure and constrained GLRT implementation.
D2. Calibrated detection thresholds and power curves for both constrained and semi-parametric statistics.
D3. Identifiability maps: which SMBHB/population/environment parameters are constrained by PTA data vs degenerate, and robust posteriors for in-band ΩGW.
D4. External consistency check against astrometric HD constraints translated to hc(f_yr)/ΩGW(f_yr).
Feasibility: 1) Addresses timing-model and cadence-induced leakage directly: Orthogonalization is performed on *effective kernels* after design-matrix projection and whitening, so separation accounts for irregular cadence, heterogeneous noise, and parameter fitting—explicitly correcting the reviewer-identified gap.
2) Robustness-first statistical design: The primary detection claim is anchored to a semi-parametric HD spectrum with weak regularization and null-calibrated thresholds; the SMBHB-constrained model is used to improve power when correct, but significance is safeguarded by mismatch injections, posterior predictive checks, and prior-sensitivity/coverage testing.
3) Identifiability replaces “unique ΩGW inference”: The proposal explicitly quantifies degeneracies from environmental coupling/eccentricity/population uncertainty, reporting only in-band ΩGW constraints and identifiable spectral summaries, avoiding overstated uniqueness.
4) EoS linkage is de-risked: The neutron-star EoS/moment-of-inertia prior is not used as a core constraint unless demonstrably informative via KL/prior-to-posterior compression and predictive-fit improvement; otherwise it is relegated to a controlled sensitivity study to avoid decorative physics or underfitting.
5) Computational scalability is explicit: Low-rank Fourier GP likelihoods with Woodbury identities and frequency-domain factorization avoid cubic scaling in total TOAs; sampling avoids RJMCMC in the primary pipeline, and convergence/diagnostics plus pre-registered null calibration prevent spurious significance from over-informative priors.
final_critique: This is an unusually sophisticated and internally consistent PTA data-analysis proposal that squarely targets a well-known bottleneck: leakage between common red processes and Hellings–Downs correlations under realistic cadence, noise, and timing-model fits. The methodological chain from timing-model marginalization, through whitening, to defining effective spatial kernels and a robustness-first GLRT is logically sound and technically credible. The strongest aspect is the insistence that orthogonality be defined in the experiment-induced inner product, not on the sky, which is a genuine conceptual advance over many existing analyses. The dual-spectrum strategy (constrained SMBHB-informed plus semi-parametric guardrail) is well motivated and directly addresses false significance under spectral mismatch. Minor deductions arise because (i) the proposal assumes that kernel orthogonalization remains numerically stable as the pulsar array grows and kernels proliferate, which is plausible but not fully stress-tested here, and (ii) the identifiability analysis, while well framed, relies heavily on Fisher/likelihood geometry without specifying clear decision thresholds for declaring parameters non-identifiable. These are refinements rather than fundamental flaws.

original_chain: energy function -> FRB 20220912A -> frequency-magnitude relationship -> FRB 20201124A -> plasma turbulence -> FRB 20201124A -> plasma turbulence -> FRB 20201124A
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: The apparent universal broken power-law in repeating-FRB burst energy functions (break near ~10^38 erg in FAST catalogs for FRB 20201124A and FRB 20220912A) is not primarily a radiative-selection artifact but the statistical signature of a strain-limited, self-organized critical (SOC) failure process in a magnetar crust whose maximum avalanche size is set by nuclear-physics-controlled yielding and crust thickness (EoS dependent). The observed frequency-magnitude relationship emerges from SOC avalanche dynamics, while the break energy corresponds to the largest connected failure patch permitted by the crust’s elastic correlation length under strong magnetic stresses. We will test this with a structurally novel methodological adaptation: replace broken-power-law fitting and hierarchical selection modeling with a physics-closed, event-sequence inversion that (i) learns a latent, time-dependent stress field (a hidden-state variable) governed by a constrained stochastic differential equation (stress loading + threshold-triggered avalanches) and (ii) maps stress drops to radio energies through a magnetospheric conversion functional constrained by energy conservation and Alfvén crossing-time causality. This ‘SOC-state-space inversion’ uses burst times + energies jointly (not energies alone) to identify whether a true maximum avalanche scale exists, and directly translates the inferred maximum correlated failure area into neutron-star crust and EoS constraints. Plasma turbulence is treated as an independent, measurable propagation layer that perturbs polarization/RM statistics but cannot by construction generate a hard maximum avalanche size in the latent stress dynamics; thus, the method mechanistically discriminates intrinsic SOC break physics from propagation effects.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Assemble uniform burst event lists for FRB 20201124A and FRB 20220912A from FAST: arrival time, fluence, width, center frequency/bandwidth, polarization products where available, and per-burst detection threshold metadata; retain burst-to-burst time ordering precisely.
1.2 Convert fluence to isotropic-equivalent energy with uncertainty propagation (distance, bandpass, spectral index priors). Construct per-burst likelihoods that retain heteroscedastic energy errors and width-dependent detectability.
1.3 For FRB 20201124A, compute RM(t) and the RM structure function, explicitly decomposing the periodic geometric component (binary-orbit sightline modulation) from the stochastic component. Extract turbulence descriptors: RM variance level, correlation time/scale, and (if possible) inertial-range slope.
1.4 For FRB 20220912A, derive propagation proxies from dynamic spectra (scattering time vs frequency, scintillation bandwidth, depolarization trends) to obtain turbulence descriptors consistent in dimensionality with 1.3.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Build a SOC state-space generative model for crustal stress.
- Latent state: a global or multi-zone stress variable x(t) representing magnetically loaded shear stress in the crust.
- Loading: dx/dt = \dot{x}_load + \sigma_x dW_t (slow drive), with \dot{x}_load constrained by magnetar spin-down/magnetic evolution timescales.
- Failure rule: when x(t) exceeds a yield threshold x_c (distributed across zones), an avalanche occurs, producing a stress drop \Delta x drawn from an SOC kernel with finite-size cutoff determined by the maximum correlated rupture area A_max.
- Crucial adaptation: A_max is not a free statistical break; it is parameterized as A_max = f(R, \Delta R_crust, \mu, \sigma_break, B) with explicit dependence on crust thickness \Delta R_crust and shear modulus \mu from candidate EoS, and breaking strain \sigma_break from nuclear pasta/microphysics priors.

2.2 Map stress drops to radio burst energies with physical closure.
- Radiated energy model: E_radio = \eta \; E_elastic(\Delta x, A, \Delta R_crust), where E_elastic is computed from elastic theory (shear energy density integrated over rupture volume), and \eta is a bounded conversion efficiency constrained by magnetospheric energetics.
- Causality constraint: impose a hard prior that burst duration/energy release is limited by Alfvén crossing time t_A \sim L/v_A and magnetospheric impedance, ruling out unphysical combinations of (A, \Delta x, E_radio) for given B and density profile.
- This creates a mechanistic guarantee: an apparent energy break can only arise from a finite A_max (intrinsic) or from a change in \eta(E) that is itself bounded by magnetospheric physics, not from arbitrary piecewise power-law fitting.

2.3 Observation model that is propagation-aware but non-degenerate with the intrinsic cutoff.
- Use a detection model based on measured widths and telescope sensitivity: P(detect|E_radio, W, \nu) from radiometer equation and pipeline thresholds.
- Incorporate plasma-turbulence effects only through independently constrained nuisance parameters that modify observed width/polarization (e.g., scattering broadening, depolarization), with priors anchored by RM structure-function/turbulence proxies (Steps 1.3–1.4).
- Structural novelty: propagation enters only the measurement channel; the latent SOC dynamics are inferred primarily from joint timing+energy statistics (including waiting-time distributions and energy–waiting-time correlations), which turbulence cannot reproduce.

2.4 Inference engine: constrained sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) with physics-projectors.
- Implement particle filtering / particle MCMC for the thresholded jump-SDE with avalanches, using “physics-projectors” that reject particles violating (i) energy conservation bounds between E_elastic and E_radio, (ii) causality via t_A, and (iii) EoS-causality (sound speed < c) and maximum-mass constraints for the adopted EoS family.
- Fit both sources jointly with shared microphysical hyperparameters (e.g., \sigma_break distribution, \eta prior family) and source-specific B-field/environment parameters.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Synthetic recovery with controlled ground truth.
- Generate mock catalogs from the SOC state-space model across a grid of (\Delta R_crust, \sigma_break, B, A_max) and add turbulence-like measurement distortions consistent with RM SF statistics. Verify unbiased recovery of A_max and EoS-linked parameters.
- Show that broken-power-law fits (baseline) spuriously recover a “universal break” even when A_max differs, whereas the SOC inversion recovers the correct source-to-source variation (or true universality).

3.2 Mechanistic discrimination tests.
- Compare models: (M1) intrinsic SOC with finite-size cutoff A_max; (M2) SOC without finite-size cutoff but with stronger propagation/detection truncation; (M3) purely phenomenological broken power law.
- Use Bayes factors / marginal likelihood via SMC, plus posterior predictive checks on: waiting-time distribution, clustering, energy–waiting-time coupling, and high-energy tail behavior.

3.3 Nuclear-physics/EoS translation.
- From posterior on A_max and elastic parameters, infer credible regions for \Delta R_crust and \mu, mapping onto EoS families consistent with causality and 2 M_sun constraints.
- Quantify how strongly the inferred maximum avalanche size constrains breaking strain \sigma_break and the presence/extent of nuclear pasta layers.

3.4 Cross-observable validation with FRB 20201124A turbulence diagnostics.
- Verify that inferred propagation nuisance parameters reproduce observed RM SF stochastic amplitude and depolarization/scattering trends, without shifting the inferred intrinsic A_max.
- Use the binary geometric RM component as an external consistency check: ensure orbital-phase-dependent RM changes do not correlate with inferred intrinsic stress state (a falsifiable non-correlation prediction if the break is intrinsic).

3.5 Robustness and reproducibility.
- Ablation: fit timing-only, energy-only, and joint timing+energy; demonstrate that only the joint SOC inversion stably identifies a finite-size cutoff.
- Release an open, unit-tested inference code and simulated catalogs covering expected FAST selection functions.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: FAST provides exceptionally large burst samples (e.g., 1,076 bursts for FRB 20220912A in 8.67 hr) enabling high-order statistics beyond energy histograms, including waiting-time and clustering measures central to SOC dynamics. Existing reports of broken power-law energy functions and earthquake-like frequency-magnitude behavior motivate an SOC/avalanche mechanism, while RM structure-function analyses for FRB 20201124A provide empirical turbulence descriptors to constrain propagation as a measurement effect.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The SOC-state-space inversion enforces conservation laws (elastic-to-radiative energy budget), causality (Alfvén crossing-time constraints), and nuclear-physics structure via EoS-dependent crust thickness and shear modulus. It directly targets high-energy astrophysics and nuclear physics by mapping an observable (maximum avalanche energy scale) onto crust microphysics and EoS families, rather than treating burst energies as black-box draws from a broken power law.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike standard broken-power-law or completeness-corrected fits, the proposed method uses joint time–energy statistics and a thresholded dynamical mechanism that uniquely predicts correlations (clustering, energy–waiting-time coupling) and a finite-size cutoff tied to crust physics. Plasma turbulence is incorporated only in the observation channel with externally anchored priors, preventing degeneracy where propagation can masquerade as an intrinsic cutoff. This yields physically interpretable posteriors on crust yielding and EoS parameters that phenomenological energy-function fitting cannot provide.
final_critique: This is an unusually sophisticated and technically ambitious proposal that demonstrates deep familiarity with FRB phenomenology, SOC theory, neutron-star crust physics, and modern Bayesian inference. The logical chain from observed broken power-law behavior to a finite-size SOC cutoff controlled by crustal microphysics is internally consistent and well motivated. The key strength is the explicit closure between latent stress dynamics, elastic energy release, magnetospheric conversion, and observation, which directly addresses the degeneracy between intrinsic physics and selection/propagation effects. Engineering resolution is high, with concrete steps for data preparation, generative modeling, inference, and validation. The main weaknesses are (i) the extreme computational and identifiability burden of particle MCMC for a thresholded jump-SDE with many tightly constrained physics projectors, which risks posterior degeneracy between A_max, conversion efficiency η, and stress-drop statistics; and (ii) the assumption that a low-dimensional (global or few-zone) stress variable can faithfully encode the spatial complexity of crustal yielding without biasing inferred A_max. These issues do not undermine feasibility but warrant modest score deductions.

original_chain: proper motion -> binary pulsar -> Galactic acceleration -> proper motion -> pulsar -> total mass -> black hole -> neutron star merger
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Binary-pulsar timing can be used to infer a Poisson-consistent Milky Way gravitational potential and, critically, a calibrated *solar-neighborhood line-of-sight acceleration/jerk model* that reduces long-term phase systematics in pulsar timing and provides a validated local reference for kinematic corrections—but it does *not* generically provide an informative luminosity-distance prior for extragalactic GW binaries. The causally correct transfer to GW/EOS inference is instead: (1) use pulsars to produce a quantified, externally validated posterior over local Galactic acceleration and Solar-system barycentric kinematic terms, and (2) use that result only as a *calibration/consistency anchor* for a separate, survey-constrained *peculiar-velocity field model* applicable to EM-identified GW hosts (or Local Group events). In the regime where host redshift is available (standard siren with counterpart) and distances are inferred via z–DL conversion, improved peculiar-velocity posteriors tighten the mapping from detector-frame to source-frame masses (M_source = M_det/(1+z)), and thereby sharpen EOS-linked prompt-collapse threshold inference (e.g., for high-total-mass systems like GW190425). Mechanistically, the proposal breaks the mass–redshift (and thus EOS/prompt-collapse) uncertainty by reducing σ_vpec and explicitly propagating that reduction through the redshift posterior; it does *not* claim to break the GW amplitude distance–inclination degeneracy except in the niche case of Galactic/Local-Group sources where Milky Way kinematics become comparable to other distance systematics.
Plan: Stage A — Pulsar-side: infer and validate the Milky Way acceleration field (kept local; no over-claiming of extragalactic leverage)
A1. Pulsar sample and data products: Compile a set of high-precision binary pulsars with (i) measured proper motions μ and uncertainties, (ii) orbital period derivatives \dot{P}_b (and timing baselines to exploit t^{-5/2} scaling where applicable), (iii) parallax when available, and (iv) systems with clean GR intrinsic \dot{P}_b modeling (e.g., analogs of PSR B1534+12; include narrow-profile MSPs analogous to PSR J1909-3744 for high timing precision). Store timing-model outputs (TEMPO2/enterprise-compatible) including sky position, binary parameters, and covariances.
A2. Forward model for \dot{P}_b decomposition (per pulsar i):
  \dot{P}_{b,obs,i} = \dot{P}_{b,GR,i}(m_1,m_2,e,P_b,...) + (\mu_i^2 d_i/c) P_{b,i} + (a_{\rm gal}(\mathbf{x}_i)\cdot \hat{n}_i/c) P_{b,i} + \dot{P}_{b,rot,i} + \epsilon_i.
Implement \dot{P}_{b,GR} with standard GR radiation-reaction and include known kinematic terms (Shklovskii; differential rotation) with consistent coordinate conventions (ICRS/Galactic) and unit checks.
A3. Poisson-consistent potential parameterization: Adopt a low-dimensional physically constrained Milky Way potential (disk + bulge + halo) where density is non-negative and integrable. Concretely:
  • Disk: double-exponential or Miyamoto–Nagai with parameters {\Sigma_0, R_d, z_d}.
  • Halo: flattened NFW or cored isothermal with {\rho_s, r_s, q}.
  • Impose priors anchored to Oort-limit measurements (mid-plane density) and contemporary rotation-curve constraints (broad, not over-informative).
Compute accelerations via gradients of \Phi(R,z), not polynomial free fits.
A4. Hierarchical inference and pooling: Fit all pulsars jointly with shared Galactic potential parameters \Theta_{MW} and per-pulsar latent variables {d_i, v_{\perp,i}} (or equivalently μ_i and d_i) using a hierarchical Bayesian model. Include parallax likelihood terms when available to validate distance recovery rather than to dominate it.
A5. Deliverable prior object (reduced dimension): From the posterior p(\Theta_{MW}|\{\dot{P}_b,\mu,\pi\}), construct a compact surrogate for the local line-of-sight acceleration a_{los}(l,b,d) and its uncertainty in the solar neighborhood (e.g., Gaussian-process emulator or spline basis with posterior covariance), explicitly limited to d \lesssim 5–10 kpc where pulsars constrain it. This object is *not* advertised as a luminosity-distance prior for extragalactic sources; it is a validated local calibration product.
A6. Validation: (i) Posterior predictive checks recovering parallax distances; (ii) reproduce Oort-limit a_z constraints; (iii) injection tests with synthetic pulsar populations in a known \Phi to quantify bias/variance in recovered a_{los}.

Stage B — Extragalactic transfer: peculiar-velocity field model (the causal bridge to source-frame mass)
B1. Define applicable regime explicitly:
  • Primary: BNS events with EM-identified host galaxy redshift z_host (standard sirens).
  • Secondary: very nearby events (Local Group / \lesssim 20–40 Mpc) where peculiar velocities materially affect z–distance conversion.
  • Not targeted: generic dark sirens without host ID (unless cross-correlation methods are added later).
B2. Host peculiar-velocity model (replaces MW potential as the extragalactic driver): Build a Bayesian peculiar-velocity field model v_pec(\mathbf{r}) constrained by galaxy redshift surveys / reconstructed density fields (e.g., a linear-theory or constrained-realization framework). Parameters include growth rate f, bias b, smoothing scale, and a stochastic dispersion term \sigma_* to absorb small-scale virial motions.
B3. Local calibration link (how pulsars enter causally): Use the pulsar-inferred local acceleration/kinematics posterior as a calibration/consistency prior on the *observer-frame* velocity field at the Solar position (e.g., constraints on local acceleration/velocity gradients and consistency with the modeled flow near the origin). This prevents unphysical local solutions in the LSS reconstruction and provides a quantified anchor for the observer-term in v_pec corrections.
B4. Construct event-specific redshift likelihood: For each GW event with a host,
  z_obs = z_cosmo(D_L;H_0,\Omega_m,...) + (v_pec,host - v_pec,obs)\cdot\hat{n}/c,
with v_pec,obs constrained by the Stage-A calibration and v_pec,host drawn from the Stage-B velocity-field posterior at the host position. This yields p(z_cosmo|z_obs, \hat{n}, \mathrm{host}) and thus p(1+z) for mass de-redshifting.

Stage C — GW/EOS inference (modular, identifiable, reduced dimension)
C1. Modularization (addresses identifiability/high dimension): Do *not* sample over \Theta_{MW} inside the GW run. Instead, ingest the reduced “prior object” from A5 (local calibration) and the velocity-field posterior hyperparameters from B2/B3.
C2. GW parameter estimation: Run standard Bayesian GW inference for BNS events to obtain posterior samples in detector-frame masses and extrinsic parameters. Keep calibration uncertainties explicit (as in standard LIGO/Virgo workflows) to allow an error-budget comparison.
C3. Source-frame mass inference via redshift posterior: For each GW posterior sample, draw (1+z) from the event-specific p(1+z) in B4 and compute source-frame masses. Quantify the reduction in \sigma_{M_source} attributable specifically to reduced \sigma_{vpec} (ablation: inflate \sigma_{vpec} or remove Stage-A calibration).
C4. EOS/prompt-collapse mapping (kept separate from distance claims): Apply EOS constraints using a TOV solver or EOS-insensitive relations with a controlled EOS hyperprior (causality, thermodynamic stability, and maximum-mass constraints). Compute prompt-collapse probability using EOS-dependent threshold relations based on source-frame total mass M_tot,source and (where available) tidal information.
C5. Mandatory quantification (Fisher/injection studies):
  • Injection grid over distances (20–300 Mpc), inclinations, and host environments to compute how much \sigma_{vpec} reduction translates into \sigma_z and \sigma_{M_source} reduction.
  • Compare magnitude against dominant terms: GW distance–inclination degeneracy, detector calibration, and host redshift measurement error.
  • Report the parameter regime where improvement is competitive (e.g., nearby events, high SNR, well-localized, secure host ID).

Stage D — Error-budget table and ablations (explicit reviewer-required deliverables)
D1. Provide an error-budget table per regime (Galactic/Local Group/nearby extragalactic) listing contributions to uncertainty in M_source and in prompt-collapse probability: GW measurement, calibration, inclination-distance degeneracy, v_pec, H_0/cosmology.
D2. Ablation suite:
  (i) velocity-field model without pulsar calibration,
  (ii) pulsar calibration with relaxed Poisson constraints,
  (iii) no pooling across pulsars,
  (iv) inflated small-scale dispersion \sigma_*.
Quantify which element tightens M_source and prompt-collapse inference.
D3. Success criteria: Demonstrate (a) unbiased recovery in injections, (b) measurable reduction in \sigma_{M_source} for the applicable regime, and (c) resulting tightening of EOS-dependent prompt-collapse boundary constraints for high-mass events (GW190425-like).
Feasibility: Causal linkage and scope control: The revised proposal explicitly limits Milky Way acceleration inference to what pulsars can constrain (local a_{los} and kinematic corrections) and removes the overstated claim that this alone breaks GW luminosity-distance degeneracies for extragalactic sources. The transfer step is reformulated into a physically correct path: host peculiar-velocity uncertainty impacts the redshift used to convert detector-frame to source-frame masses, which directly controls EOS/prompt-collapse inference.

Quantifiability: The plan includes mandatory Fisher/injection studies to compute the achievable reduction in σ_vpec and propagate it to σ_z and σ_{M_source}, then compare it against calibration and inclination-distance uncertainties. This directly addresses the reviewer demand for a competitive error-budget demonstration.

Identifiability and computation: The pipeline is modularized into two stages with a reduced-dimensional surrogate “prior object” exported from the pulsar analysis, avoiding a prohibitively high-dimensional unified sampler over Milky Way potential + EOS + GW parameters. Identifiability is enforced through ablations that isolate whether (and when) pulsar calibration measurably tightens source-frame mass.

Empirical anchoring: The pulsar-side methodology is supported by demonstrated capability to infer distances/velocities via \dot{P}_b kinematic decomposition (proper motion/Shklovskii) with improving precision over time baselines, and by direct-measurement approaches linking timing to Galactic acceleration and Oort-limit constraints. On the GW side, high-total-mass events (GW190425-like) make prompt-collapse probability extremely sensitive to source-frame total mass, so any credible reduction in mass de-redshifting uncertainty yields disproportionate leverage on the collapse boundary—provided the regime (nearby, host-identified) is respected.
final_critique: The proposal is methodologically careful about not over-claiming extragalactic distance leverage from Milky Way dynamics, which substantially improves logical consistency relative to common failure modes. Stage A is technically plausible (Poisson-consistent potential; •Pb decomposition; hierarchical pooling; validation/injections) and the modularization (exported surrogate rather than monolithic joint sampling) is a strong engineering choice. The main weakness is quantitative: the incremental information provided by pulsar-inferred *acceleration/jerk* for the *observer term* in peculiar-velocity corrections is likely to be small compared with existing constraints on the solar motion relative to the CMB and local-flow reconstructions, and the proposal does not yet demonstrate that Stage-A improves the dominant uncertainty entering z-corrections (typically host/environment peculiar velocity and non-linear dispersion). Additionally, the connection to 'jerk' is asserted but not operationalized in the •Pb model (which is primarily sensitive to acceleration projections and kinematic biases); if jerk is intended to mitigate long-term phase systematics, it needs explicit timing-model pathways and identifiability analysis. Finally, while the EOS/prompt-collapse motivation is sound, the proposal needs a clearer forecast showing that plausible reductions in σ_vpec (after including σ_* and survey systematics) actually move the prompt-collapse odds for GW190425-like systems beyond what tidal/selection/calibration uncertainties already dominate.

original_chain: Z source -> waiting time -> neutron star -> sub-thermal timescale -> neutron star -> SGR 1806-20 -> asymmetric outflow -> expansion
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A single microphysical control parameter—time-dependent effective rigidity set by crustal yield plus core phase-transition-driven moment-of-inertia anomalies—simultaneously shapes (i) the waiting-time distribution of impulsive magnetar energy releases and (ii) the degree of one-sided (asymmetric) relativistic ejecta that produces the observed expansion/deceleration in the SGR 1806-20 radio afterglow; the same parameter predicts a population-level spin-evolution “waiting-time pile-up” in accreting Z sources when they traverse a deconfinement critical line. Methodological adaptation: we will modify standard Bayesian hierarchical inference of transient outflows by replacing ad hoc priors/likelihoods with a physics-constrained, piecewise-deterministic state-space model whose latent state evolves under torque balance (for Z sources) and magnetic stress accumulation (for magnetars), but whose jump (burst/flare) hazard and ejecta anisotropy are jointly generated by an EOS- and phase-transition-aware constitutive law that enforces causality, energy-momentum conservation, and TOV-consistent compactness. Mechanism: (1) near a deconfinement transition, dI/dΩ changes sign/steepness, producing a spindown “stall” (enhanced waiting time) in Z sources; (2) the same stiff/soft response of dense matter controls how quickly magnetic/elastic stresses reach yield, setting a non-Poisson (approximately lognormal) waiting-time distribution; (3) once yield occurs, asymmetric slip localized to one hemisphere launches a momentum-imbalanced outflow whose centroid proper motion and anisotropic expansion follow directly from the conserved impulse imparted to the external shock, explaining SGR 1806-20’s 0.26c centroid motion and contemporaneous expansion deceleration.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Compile Z-source timing/spectral tracks for a representative sample (including known Z sources with long-term spin/torque proxies where available), extracting segment-wise torque indicators and constructing empirical “residence time” (waiting time) along the Z track (HB/NB/FB) with uncertainty.
1.2 Compile SGR 1806-20 burst catalog waiting times (including the active 2003–2004 phase) and the 2004 giant flare radio afterglow observables: time series of angular size (major/minor axes), centroid proper motion, flux evolution, polarization fraction/angle.
1.3 Define a family of dense-matter EOS parameterizations that explicitly include/omit a first-order deconfinement transition (e.g., spectral or piecewise-polytrope for hadronic sector + constant-sound-speed quark sector), enforcing: (i) dp/dε <= c^2 (causality), (ii) thermodynamic stability, (iii) TOV maximum mass >= 2 Msun, and (iv) continuity conditions at the transition.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Adaptation A (physics-constrained hazard model): Build a piecewise-deterministic Markov process (PDMP) latent state x(t) = {Ω(t), B(t), σ(t), I(Ω;EOS), Q(t)} where σ is crustal stress proxy and Q indicates proximity to a phase boundary. Between events, evolve deterministically:
- Accreting Z sources: dΩ/dt = [N_acc(Ṁ,Z-state) - N_mag(Ω,B)]/I(Ω;EOS) with I computed from TOV+Hartle-Thorne slow-rotation or calibrated GR fits; include deconfinement-induced I(Ω) nonlinearity.
- Magnetar: dσ/dt = F(B,Ω,thermal state) representing stress accumulation from magnetic field evolution and spin-down.
Events occur with hazard λ(t) = λ0 * exp[g(σ/σ_y(EOS), dI/dΩ, thermal proxy)], where σ_y is EOS-dependent yield threshold (effective rigidity), producing non-Poisson waiting times.
2.2 Adaptation B (impulse-conserving asymmetric outflow module): Replace standard isotropic afterglow fits with an anisotropic thin-shell shock model where the ejecta momentum distribution is expanded in low-order spherical harmonics and truncated to a dipole+quadrupole consistent with observed 2:1 axis ratio. Enforce global energy-momentum conservation: total impulse P_ej and energy E_ej satisfy E_ej >= P_ej^2/(2M_ej) and shock evolution obeys d(M_sw v)/dt = -dP_rad/dt with radiative losses bounded. Couple the dipole amplitude to the same yield variable that sets λ(t): A1 ∝ (localized slip fraction) = h(σ/σ_y).
2.3 Joint hierarchical inference: Fit Z-source residence-time data + magnetar waiting-time series + SGR 1806-20 radio morphology/centroid/polarization using a single hyperparameter set controlling EOS (including transition strength), σ_y(EOS), and mapping coefficients. Use Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with constrained parameter transforms to guarantee causality/TOV constraints; compute I(Ω) and compactness self-consistently per EOS draw.
2.4 Posterior predictive checks targeted to the chain: predict (i) enhanced waiting times/pile-up region for Z sources near the critical line, (ii) lognormal-like waiting-time statistics for SGR bursts with parameter drift during active phase, (iii) synchronized centroid motion + expansion deceleration for the giant flare afterglow when dipole impulse dominates, and (iv) polarization evolution consistent with an elongated, one-sided shock.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Model comparison: Bayes factors / information criteria between (i) no phase transition vs transition EOS families, and (ii) isotropic vs impulse-conserving anisotropic outflow, and (iii) memoryless Poisson hazard vs PDMP hazard.
3.2 Identifiability and robustness: synthetic-data injection studies varying distance, ambient density gradients, and observational cadence to confirm recovery of transition-induced dI/dΩ features and outflow dipole amplitude.
3.3 Physical consistency audits: verify energy budget against observed GF energetics; ensure inferred ejecta mass/energy do not violate magnetar magnetic free energy; ensure inferred Z-source torque histories remain consistent with accretion luminosity bounds.
3.4 Falsifiable predictions: (i) Z sources should cluster in residence time at luminosities/track positions corresponding to Ω where dI/dΩ anomalies occur; (ii) magnetars with stronger inferred anisotropy in radio afterglows should exhibit broader/heavier-tailed waiting-time distributions during active phases; (iii) if future magnetar GFs show smaller centroid motion, the model predicts correspondingly reduced dipole impulse and a measurable shift toward more Poisson-like waiting times.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 1 provides a concrete mechanism for increased waiting time in Z sources via moment-of-inertia changes across deconfinement transitions; Asset 5 provides high-quality constraints on asymmetric outflow, centroid proper motion, and decelerating expansion in SGR 1806-20; Assets 2–3 ground waiting-time and sub-thermal-timescale dynamics in neutron-star contexts, motivating a non-Poisson hazard tied to internal stress/transfer processes.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The key adaptation is replacing phenomenological waiting-time fits and isotropic afterglow models with a single EOS-aware PDMP + impulse-conserving anisotropic shock model. This directly encodes domain constraints (TOV structure, causality, conservation laws) into the inference architecture, rather than learning black-box correlations.
3. Comparative Advantage: Standard approaches separately fit burst waiting times (often purely statistical) and radio afterglows (often isotropic or weakly anisotropic) and treat Z-source clustering as independent phenomenology. The proposed joint, physics-constrained state-space model links all three through a mechanistic latent variable (EOS/rigidity/phase-transition control), enabling stronger EOS discrimination and providing cross-validation: EOS parameters must simultaneously explain Z-source residence-time pile-ups and SGR 1806-20’s asymmetric expansion/centroid motion. This multi-dataset constraint should sharply reduce degeneracies (e.g., ambient density vs energy vs anisotropy) that limit current inferences.
final_critique:
This is an ambitious, technically sophisticated proposal that tightly integrates neutron-star EOS physics, timing statistics, and relativistic outflow dynamics. The strongest aspect is the explicit enforcement of causality, TOV consistency, and energy–momentum conservation directly inside the inference architecture, which is rarely attempted and represents a genuine methodological advance. The logical chain linking deconfinement-induced dI/dΩ anomalies to Z-source residence-time pile-ups is sound and grounded in prior spin-evolution theory. Likewise, the impulse-based explanation of the SGR 1806-20 centroid motion is physically credible and better constrained than ad hoc anisotropy parameters.

Score deductions arise primarily from identifiability and empirical leverage concerns. Long-term torque proxies for Z sources are sparse and indirect, raising the risk that inferred waiting-time pile-ups may be weakly constrained relative to the EOS hyperparameters. The assumption that a single effective rigidity/yield parameter can quantitatively control both crustal failure statistics in magnetars and accretion-driven spin evolution in Z sources, while not inconsistent, remains only partially justified at the microphysical level and may introduce degeneracies that even joint inference cannot fully break. Finally, the PDMP hazard functional form, though physically motivated, introduces multiple coupled nonlinear dependencies whose uniqueness of inference is not yet demonstrated.

original_chain: coalescence -> electromagnetic counterpart -> neutron star - black hole binary -> localization region -> neutron star - black hole binary
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Neutron star–black hole (NSBH) coalescences produce detectable electromagnetic (EM) counterparts primarily when the neutron star is tidally disrupted outside the black hole ISCO, and that same disruption changes (i) the remnant/ejecta properties that power kilonova/afterglow emission and (ii) the terminal gravitational-wave (GW) signal morphology at high frequencies. The key methodological claim is not that a >700 Hz “cutoff” is always measurable, but that a rigorously specified, bias-controlled generative model—explicitly separating a latent disruption state D and ejecta properties E—enables two complementary inference pathways: (A) a conservative GW-only pathway where disruption affects inference only through EoS-consistent priors and (when identifiable) a statistically validated high-frequency disruption component, and (B) a GW+EM pathway where EM data constrain E (and thus D) without double-counting NR fits. This architecture overcomes reviewer-noted risks by (1) enforcing conditional-independence structure so NR-calibrated mappings are used once via shared latent variables rather than twice as pseudo-independent evidence, (2) activating the waveform-level disruption imprint only in a quantified identifiability regime (network/SNR/bandwidth threshold) that is robust to calibration and known waveform systematics (precession, higher modes, PSD uncertainty), and (3) improving follow-up efficiency primarily via physically consistent reweighting of distance–inclination and q–spin–EoS degeneracies into an explicit sky-dependent detectability map, rather than claiming unconditional localization area reductions. The measurable outcome is a ranked, telescope-specific EM detectability sky map and a set of preregistered ablation results that state exactly when (and why) EoS constraints, disruption-imprint waveform terms, and EM coupling improve 3D localization and reduce false-positive follow-up burden for HLV/HKLV/HIKLV networks.
Plan: Step 0 — Define a bias-controlled generative model (graphical model + factorized likelihood).
0.1 Latent variables and observed data.
- Intrinsic binary parameters: θ_int = {m_NS, m_BH, χ_BH (magnitude), tilt β, spin azimuth, (optionally) χ_NS}, extrinsic parameters: θ_ext = {α, δ, d_L, ι, ψ, t_c, φ_c}.
- Neutron-star EoS hyperparameters: ϕ_EoS via spectral parameterization; derived NS structure: {R(m_NS), C(m_NS), Λ(m_NS)}.
- Latent disruption state: D ∈ {0,1} (non-disruptive / disruptive).
- Latent ejecta and remnant properties: E = {M_ej, v_ej, X_lan (or Y_e), disk mass M_disk, polar/equatorial partition}, and jet/afterglow parameters J (optional): {E_jet, θ_j, n_ISM, ε_e, ε_B}.
- Observables: GW strain data d_GW from detector network; EM photometry/spectra/upper limits d_EM with cadence/censoring.

0.2 NR-informed maps as conditional distributions (used once).
- Disruption probability model: p(D=1 | θ_int, ϕ_EoS, κ_NR) where κ_NR indexes an NR-fit family; built from R_tid/R_ISCO with a calibrated transition width. This is not a delta-function threshold; it is a probabilistic classifier with uncertainty.
- Ejecta model: p(E | D, θ_int, ϕ_EoS, κ_NR) (NR-calibrated fits + intrinsic scatter).
- EM radiative-transfer surrogate: p(d_EM | E, θ_ext, κ_RT) with κ_RT an RT/surrogate family index; includes detection/non-detection likelihood with survey depth and cadence.

0.3 GW likelihood with optional disruption-imprint component under identifiability gating.
- Baseline: p(d_GW | θ_int, θ_ext, ϕ_EoS, κ_wf, κ_cal, κ_PSD) using waveform family κ_wf (including precession/higher modes variants) and calibration/PSD nuisance parameters.
- Disruption-imprint augmentation: introduce a physically motivated spectral modification S(f; θ_int, ϕ_EoS, D, κ_NR) applied only if the data support it (see Step 2). Importantly, the imprint’s amplitude is not freely fit without penalty: it is tied to θ_int and ϕ_EoS through D with explicit uncertainty.

0.4 Full joint posterior with selection effects.
Write the hierarchical posterior (schematically):

p(θ_int, θ_ext, ϕ_EoS, D, E, κ_NR, κ_RT, κ_wf, κ_cal, κ_PSD | d_GW, d_EM, S_GW, S_EM)
∝ p(d_GW | θ_int, θ_ext, ϕ_EoS, D, κ_NR, κ_wf, κ_cal, κ_PSD)
  × p(d_EM | E, θ_ext, κ_RT)
  × p(E | D, θ_int, ϕ_EoS, κ_NR)
  × p(D | θ_int, ϕ_EoS, κ_NR)
  × p(θ_int, θ_ext) p(ϕ_EoS) p(κ_NR) p(κ_RT) p(κ_wf) p(κ_cal) p(κ_PSD)
  × [α_sel(θ_int, θ_ext, E)]^{-1}.

Selection factor α_sel accounts for:
- GW selection: P(det_GW | θ_int, θ_ext, κ_PSD, network) via injection-based efficiency or semi-analytic SNR thresholding.
- EM selection (if conditioning on EM-triggered follow-up or detection): P(followed-up/identified | sky position, depth, cadence, host extinction) and censoring via upper limits.

This factorization prevents double-counting: NR information enters only through p(D|…) and p(E|D, …) (shared latent variables), while GW and EM data contribute through separate likelihoods p(d_GW|…) and p(d_EM|…).

Step 1 — Data/model assembly with explicit domain coverage and OOD safeguards.
1.1 Simulation suite.
- Generate NSBH populations over q = m_BH/m_NS, BH spin magnitude |χ_BH|, tilt β, m_NS, sky position, distance, inclination; ensure coverage matching expected detection-weighted priors.
- Include networks HLV, HKLV, HIKLV; use realistic PSDs and calibration envelopes; include multiple epochs if relevant.

1.2 EoS prior with hard constraints.
- Spectral EoS parameterization p(ϕ_EoS) with constraints: causality (c_s ≤ c), thermodynamic stability (dP/dε > 0), M_max ≥ 2.0 M☉, continuity to low-density nuclear-theory constraints.
- Compute derived Λ(m_NS), C(m_NS) with uncertainty propagation.

1.3 NR-fit families and training-domain documentation.
- Curate multiple NR-based fit families κ_NR for (i) disruption criteria/classifier, (ii) ejecta/disk mass fits.
- For each κ_NR, explicitly record training domain bounds in (q, |χ_BH|, β, m_NS, EoS compactness range) and published uncertainties.

1.4 Out-of-distribution (OOD) diagnostics and conservative fallback.
- Implement an OOD score for each posterior sample (e.g., distance to convex hull / density under a normalizing-flow trained on fit-domain coordinates).
- Policy: if OOD probability exceeds a preregistered threshold (e.g., >5% posterior mass OOD), automatically (a) widen NR-fit scatter, (b) downweight disruption-imprint contribution, and (c) revert to baseline GW PE for low-latency products while flagging “extrapolation” status.

Step 2 — Quantify identifiability of the high-frequency disruption imprint before using it.
2.1 Competing hypotheses and nested models.
- H0: no disruption imprint in GW (baseline waveform with tides/precession/higher modes as appropriate).
- H1: disruption imprint present with D-linked spectral modification S(f), including calibrated uncertainty.
Compute Bayes factors B_10 and/or posterior odds for D using reversible-jump MCMC or product-space methods.

2.2 Fisher and injection-based Bayes-factor studies across systematics.
- Vary network (HLV/HKLV/HIKLV), SNR, effective bandwidth, inclination, calibration uncertainty, PSD uncertainty.
- Include waveform systematics: compare κ_wf families that add precession and higher modes; include alternative tidal prescriptions.
- Output: a preregistered “recoverability map” in (SNR, f_high, q, |χ_BH|, β) giving probability of correctly identifying imprint (true positive at fixed false-alarm).

2.3 Explicit activation threshold.
- Define a decision rule for enabling disruption-imprint inference in low latency, e.g.:
  - require network SNR ≥ 25 AND effective bandwidth such that cumulative SNR above 600–800 Hz exceeds a threshold (computed per event), AND Bayes factor ln B_10 ≥ 3 under calibration/PSD-marginalized analysis.
- If threshold not met, enforce imprint-off (H0) and restrict disruption information to prior-level physics (EoS + disruption probability) and/or EM data.

Step 3 — Inference architecture for localization and EM detectability without biasing GW likelihood.
3.1 Two-stage, bias-controlled pipeline.
Stage A (GW-only baseline):
- Perform standard PE with calibration/PSD marginalization; obtain posterior samples over θ_int, θ_ext, ϕ_EoS (if doing EoS-aware priors) under H0.

Stage B (physics-informed reweighting + optional imprint term):
- Reweight GW posterior samples by p(D|θ_int,ϕ_EoS,κ_NR) and (if imprint is activated) by the validated likelihood ratio from H1/H0 computed consistently (not by injecting an ad hoc penalty).
- This “reweighting” does not alter the GW likelihood; it updates the posterior via an explicit hierarchical prior/mixture model.

3.2 EM coupling and counterpart detectability map.
- For each posterior sample, draw (or marginalize) E ~ p(E|D, θ_int, ϕ_EoS, κ_NR).
- Generate predicted light curves via RT surrogate family κ_RT and compute detection likelihoods for specific facilities/cadences; incorporate non-detections as censoring constraints.
- Produce sky-pixel products:
  - P_det_EM(Ω) = ∫ P(det | E, d_L, ι, Ω, instrument) p(E, d_L, ι | Ω, d_GW, …) dE dd_L dι.
This yields a ranked detectability sky map over the GW localization region (not merely smaller contours).

3.3 Treatment of distance–inclination and q–spin–EoS degeneracies.
- Quantify when disruption information breaks degeneracies by reporting mutual information / KL divergence between baseline and updated posteriors in {d_L, ι} and {q, χ_BH, C}.
- Report changes in searched volume and in the posterior mass at small d_L (relevant for EM brightness) rather than only 2D sky area.

Step 4 — Preregistered ablations and validation metrics (mandatory).
4.1 Ablation matrix (preregistered).
(A) EoS-constrained priors only: enforce p(ϕ_EoS) constraints; no disruption imprint; EM not used.
(B) Waveform disruption-imprint only: allow H1 vs H0 with identifiability gating; EoS fixed/broad; EM not used.
(C) EM coupling only: baseline GW PE + p(D|…) + p(E|…) + RT surrogate to make detectability maps; no imprint term.
(D) Full model: (A)+(B)+(C) with OOD safeguards.

4.2 Metrics.
- Localization: 2D area (90% credible), 3D volume (90%), “searched volume–time” for follow-up.
- EM follow-up utility: counterpart recovery fraction at fixed telescope time; expected number of unrelated transients followed (false-positive burden) under realistic transient rates.
- Bias checks: coverage tests (credible interval calibration) for sky position, distance, inclination.

4.3 Robustness to systematics.
- Repeat with multiple κ_wf waveform families (including precession/higher modes) and multiple κ_NR and κ_RT families; marginalize over κ indices or report sensitivity.
- Calibration/PSD uncertainty: include nuisance parameters; verify the imprint Bayes factor is not spuriously driven by calibration residuals.

Step 5 — Low-latency implementation with conservative fallbacks.
5.1 Deliverable products within minutes–hours.
- Product 1: standard GW skymap (baseline).
